MR. VILLENEUVE (ROBERVAL)    PROTEST AGAINST TELEVISION DESIGNATION OF LAKE ST. JOHN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege to protest against the T.V. program "Pays et Merveilles" carried last night over the C.B.C. network and which had as its guest the president of the Saguenay historical society.
In the course of that program, a certain controversial theory was brought up with regard to a so-called kingdom of the Saguenay. The guest in question held the view that this area and the Saguenay district are one and the same. I wish to go on record as protesting against this statement since it tends to describe as a single area several different areas including the Lake St. John district, where I live, which has never gone under any other name but that of Lake St. John.
On behalf of my fellow citizens in the area, which comprises the present constituencies of Lake St. John and Roberval, I wish to protest to the C.B.C. authorities against this sabotaging of a name for which I have the greatest regard, a feeling which I share with my electors and with all those who live in this fine Lake St. John area. We wish to defend the true meaning of a designation which has been consecrated by over one hundred years of history and which is widely known even beyond the borders of Canada. We refuse to let the area be called otherwise than by the name which it has always had ever since there have been people living there, that is the Lake St. John area.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ELIGIBILITY OF SCALLOP AND LOBSTER FISHERMEN FOR BOUNTY
speechtext: would like to ask the Minister of Fisheries a question. Will the minister advise the house if it is possible to add the names of fishermen engaged in the catching of scallops and lobsters to the list of deep sea fishermen receiving the fishing bounty?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. Macl.ean (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: ELIGIBILITY OF SCALLOP AND LOBSTER FISHERMEN FOR BOUNTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the short answer to the question is no, but perhaps I might be permitted to give some explanation as to the reason for that answer. The bounty paid to fishermen in the four provinces-Quebec and the three maritime provinces-arose as the result of a treaty made in Washington in 1871 between the government of Britain on the one hand and the government of the United States on the other, under which each nation granted to the other certain rights for its fishermen to fish in each other's territorial waters-in the case of Canada in the territorial waters on the east coast, and in the case of the United States the territorial waters as far south as the 39th parallel.
It was considered that the concessions made on behalf of Canada were greater than those made by the United States, so the terms of the treaty provided that a commission should be set up to arrive at the difference in value. This was done. The commission sat in Halifax and made an award known as the Halifax award, under which the United States paid to Britain the sum of $5,500,000. This was handed over by Britain to Canada and Newfoundland. Of this sum I believe just over $1 million was paid to Newfoundland and almost $4,500,000 to Canada.
This amount was considered by the Canadian government to be owned by all Canadians, and it was placed in the consolidated fund; but as the result of objections from the Atlantic provinces a bill was passed-an act now known as the Deep Sea Fisheries Act

under which a bounty was paid to fishermen. But since the treaty has from the very beginning specifically excluded shad, salmon, shellfish, and fish caught in rivers or the estuaries of rivers, the whole basis on which the award is made specifically

excludes that type of fishery, so it is considered impossible to pay any bounty now with respect to shellfish or lobster fishing of any kind.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED FAILURE TO PROVIDE ASSISTANCE TO REFUGEES
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked me a question reported at page 1825 of Hansard, with regard to a press story about non-payment of accounts for rental accommodation of refugees in Calgary. I now have available a preliminary report on the situation.
I am advised by our Calgary office that they do not have any outstanding rental accounts in which the church named in the article is involved, nor has this church approached the Calgary office for payment.

The head of the family is presently employed, earning $45 a week. Because of the numerous requests a member of the Catholic counselling service was asked to investigate. He reported, in effect, that the financial difficulties of this family are somewhat of their own making. They have been purchasing items such as a television set and a record player, and they also own a second hand Austin car. It was recommended by the investigator that they be given no further assistance from our department.
There was only one rental account for this family in March of this year, and it was brought about because they were living with another family and broke up their living quarters because of family problems. When this family sought new quarters we were asked to pay for their rental. However, no bill for this has ever been received. I think the hon. member will probably agree that under the circumstances reported there is not any very urgent necessity for us to intervene in connection with that particular family.
With regard to the other 20 accounts outstanding which are mentioned in the article, a full report is expected from the assistant district superintendent in Winnipeg.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON ADMISSION OF NEEDY EXSERVICEMEN TO DEPARTMENTAL HOSPITALS
speechtext:
I should like to reply to a question which was asked me yesterday by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). His question was:
Has the minister received letters from veterans, including one named Brooks, complaining of the fact that while immigrants and in some cases United States personnel are admitted to Shaughnessy hospital, certain veterans are denied admission?
Can the minister assure the house that no needy veterans requiring treatment will be denied admission to departmental hospitals?
The answer to the first part of the question is that I have received a letter from Mr. David Brooks requesting that the means test be removed from the operation of section 13 of the veterans treatment regulations. I have not received letters from veterans complaining about being denied admission to Shaughnessy hospital.
The answer to the second part of the question is that I can assure the house that no veteran who is eligible under any section of the veterans treatment regulations and who does require treatment is ever denied admission to departmental hospitals.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON ADMISSION OF NEEDY EXSERVICEMEN TO DEPARTMENTAL HOSPITALS
speechtext: have a supplementary question. Would the minister inform the house why it is that those who are not eligible for admission are referred by his own officials to the provincial authorities to be taken care of?

maintopic: STATEMENT ON ADMISSION OF NEEDY EXSERVICEMEN TO DEPARTMENTAL HOSPITALS
speechtext:
I do not know of any such cases. The hon. member has spoken about those who had not the means. I might say that under the veterans treatment regulations as they are at present, any eligible veteran whose income is below $960-and that is an adjusted income; exemptions are made for wife and children which are taken off the true income and he is admitted under the adjusted income-he can have free hospitalization. For adjusted annual incomes from $960 to $1,000 the maximum charge is $20 for twelve months; he does not have to pay any more. From $1,000 to $1,100 it is $33.
I am not going to read the complete list. I point this out to show that the charge is adjusted according to the income of the veteran, and our information is that these veterans with low incomes are not denied hospitalization. We have received no complaints in this connection except from the hon. member.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON POLICY RESPECTING SATELLITE STATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the last time hon. members had an opportunity to discuss defence matters in detail was in June and July of 1956, when the estimates of the Department of National Defence were before the house and approved. Since that time there have been a number of important changes

of a military and strategic nature. As this is a new house in which there are a number of new members it might be helpful if I say something about our defence commitments as they presently exist in the light of these changes.
Before I do so, however, I would like to make reference to my predecessor in this office, the former hon. member for Vancouver Centre. The brief period during which I have been Minister of National Defence has given me an understanding of the problems he had to face. Despite the onerous duties which were his lot Mr. Campney never failed to treat inquiries from me with courtesy, a practice I shall hope to follow. While we were not always satisfied with the replies, he did endeavour to obtain answers to those inquiries as quickly as possible. In the house we may have had differences over the shape of Canada's defence policy, but we were in full agreement as to the need of such a policy. I understand that Mr. Campney has now returned to his law practice in Vancouver, and I am sure all of us here wish him well in his profession.
I would also like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the senior service officers and the civilian heads of branches in the department. Since assuming office I have received the utmost co-operation and assistance from them all, and I know that without their help and support my job as minister would have been a great deal more difficult to carry out.
Our defence policy is, of course, to provide for the security of Canada. We believe the best way to achieve this aim is through membership in a collective defence organization such as NATO. While our contributions to this organization at present constitute our main defence commitments, we are fully aware of the importance of the United Nations and we will continue to assist the United Nations to attain its objectives in every possible way.
A large number of Canadian servicemen, over 900 in fact, form part of the United Nations emergency force in the Middle East, and we have supplied some 130 personnel of our armed services for the truce commission in Indo-China, the United Nations truce supervisory organization in Palestine and the truce team in Kashmir. Our membership in this NATO regional alliance is in no way contrary to the spirit of the United Nations organization. Article 51 of the charter reads in part:
Nothing in the present charter shall impair the inherent right of individual or collective self defence.
Supply-National Defence
By forming this unique organization the NATO countries have assisted the United Nations in realizing its aim of preventing any further encroachments by aggressive nations. In an alliance such as NATO collective defence can be achieved along the most economical lines by the partners contributing the kind of forces they can best produce and equip. In this way each partner is not required to have in existence all types and varieties of forces. We can do our share in the alliance by raising, equipping and training the type of force to which we are best suited and which can be supplied in the main from our own Canadian industry.
The primary military aim of NATO is to prevent war. The best way to achieve this aim is to make it clear to any potential enemy that war would be so disastrous that it must not be contemplated. In a future major conflict there will be neither victim nor vanquished, only death and destruction of such magnitude that civilization may well be ended. The essence of the NATO concept is, therefore, the idea of a deterrent. It is important that other countries know that we in NATO have the ability to retaliate immediately following any aggressive act.
The widely dispersed aircraft of the United States strategic air command, together with the V-bombers of the United Kingdom, on account of their great flexibility form a formidable retaliatory force. As General Norstad said recently, it is beyond practical limits to eliminate all our bases simultaneously notwithstanding the advent of the ballistic and other missiles.
In Canada our main contribution to this deterrent is to provide protection both for these retaliatory forces and for the industrial power of the North American continent. To this end we have established the early warning lines and air defence command.
I might say a word about Canada's commitments to NATO in terms of men and material. We have 12 squadrons of interceptor aircraft in Europe, eight of which are equipped with Sabres and four with CF-lOO's. These squadrons are formed into four wings and are located at Zweibrucken and Soellin-gen in Germany and Marville and Grosten-quin in France with divisional headquarters at Metz. Some 5,800 airmen are employed in flying and servicing these aircraft and in the performance of other duties necessary for the maintenance of the efficiency of the division. These young airmen are on duty every hour of every day 365 days in the year.
Also stationed in Germany at Soest, Hemer and Werl is the Canadian infantry brigade group made up of over 5,000 men, supported

Supply-National Defence by an armoured regiment equipped with Centurion tanks. The role of this group is to assist in the protection of western Europe by delaying any advance that might be made by enemy ground forces. By having these defensive forces in the field we compel a would-be aggressor to concentrate sufficient forces to overcome our shield, and by building up such a concentration to reveal his aggressive intentions.
Our naval contribution to NATO is not inconsiderable. Forty fighting ships and 50 maritime aircraft are earmarked for the maritime forces of the supreme allied commander, Atlantic. Hon. members will know that since 1951 we have also made available to our allies equipment valued at over $1 billion through the mutual aid program and have undertaken the training of over 5,000 pilots and navigators from member nations of the organization. Only last week ceremonies took place at Sydney, Nova Scotia, at which five Bangor-type coastal escorts were handed over to our NATO ally, Turkey. These will be followed early next year by a further five Bangors and by four bay-class minesweepers. These, then, are some of our direct commitments to NATO.
The North American continent is an integral part of the NATO area, and we are assisting very considerably in its defence. The, early warning system, built up over the years, is operated to enable our interceptor aircraft to take the necessary action against the intrusion of manned bomber aircraft. Such bomber aircraft are in operation now, and we believe that such manned aircraft will be in operation for several more years. It is felt that even when the ballistic and other guided missiles come into operation they will complement rather than replace manned bombers and interceptors for some time to come.
I might say that intensive studies are being undertaken by Canadian scientists, working in close collaboration with our allies, to develop defences against such future missiles. At the same time, however, we must be prepared to deal with offensive weapons now in operation, and it is against such weapons that our defences on the North American continent have been built up. Of the three radar lines which work as a unit, Canada operates the "Pinetree" line jointly with the United States. The mid-Canada line was built and is operated wholly by Canada. The D.E.W. line was constructed and is operated by the United States. Backing up these radar lines are nine squadrons of CF-100 aircraft which are on the alert 24 hours every day.

The air defence systems of this continent have recently been completely integrated by the establishment of a joint headquarters at Colorado Springs, with a United States commander and a Canadian deputy. Of course the effectiveness of such integration has already been demonstrated in Europe, where our forces are under the operational control of General Norstad, the supreme allied commander in Europe; and in the Atlantic where in war our ships and maritime aircraft, earmarked for the NATO naval force, would come under the supreme allied commander, Atlantic, who also has fully integrated headquarters in which Canadian officers are serving. In order to improve the capabilities of the air defence forces of Canada and the United States to support the collective security of NATO and thereby provide a greater deterrent to war, the air defence of North America is now considered as a single problem.
The importance to the NATO alliance of the United States strategic air command, nuclear retaliatory forces, and the industrial capacity of Canada and the United States makes it imperative that the most effective and efficient defence system be provided. Prior to the formation of the North American air defence command there was the closest possible co-operation and liaison between the air defence forces of Canada and the United States. The various agreements reached between the services and approved by the two governments provide for cross-border intercepts whereby the forces of one country can intercept the enemy in the territory of the other. The conditions under which intercepts could take place were clearly defined by the governments of both countries, and consequently United States aircraft operating over Canadian territory are governed by Canadian rules of engagement.
In planning their air defence systems our two countries attempted to achieve the closest possible degree of uniformity. This, however, was not always possible and often unilateral decisions, particularly in long-range planning, resulted in less effective air defence forces and equipment. The realization that duplication in planning and harmful unilateral decisions were sometimes taking place led to a study of ways and means to improve the air defence system.
The Canadian and United States chiefs of staff directed that a study of the problem be undertaken by the joint military study group, comprising senior officials of the three services and scientific agencies of both countries. This group recommended that a more effective air defence system would be achieved by integrating operational control of all air defence

forces under one joint headquarters. Subsequently the governments of Canada and the United States approved this recommendation in principle, and an integrated headquarters called North American air defence command was formed. This joint Canada-United States headquarters, known as NORAD, has been organized on principles that were devised and which operated satisfactorily during world war II for joint and combined commands.
Its responsibilities are as follows. First, in peacetime, it is developing plans and procedures that would be used in war. These plans and procedures are to be agreed to in peacetime and will be ready for immediate use in an emergency. They will be reviewed, amended or improved by the chiefs of staff of both countries, and government approval will be sought before any plans are implemented. It will be responsible for the general pattern of training and the general supervision of practice exercises in order to ensure the readiness of the forces and facilities in time of emergency.
Second, in time of war it will be responsible for the direction of the air defence operations in accordance with the plans and procedures which have been agreed upon in peacetime. As the agreed plans and procedures have been worked out in peacetime, there will be little that the NORAD commanders will be able to do in the first few hours of war except to reinforce the most threatened areas with whatever additional fighter aircraft and missiles become available after the battle is opened. These in the main will be United States forces, as Canada does not maintain immediately ready reserves.
The officer appointed to fill the position of commander in chief, North American air defence, was made responsible to the governments of both countries for the air defence of North America, and to report directly to the United States joint chiefs of staff and the Canadian chiefs of staff committee. All plans for the deployment and employment of air defence forces must be approved by the chiefs of staff and, when necessary, Ijy the governments of both countries.
The terms of reference which outline the responsibilities of the commander in chief of NORAD and the organization required to exercise operational control are under study at the present time and will be approved before a formal agreement between the two governments is finalized. Until the agreement is formalized, NORAD is operating on an interim arrangement whereby a small staff of R.C.A.F. officers headed by Air Marshal Slemon are working on the preparation of the 96698-121
Supply-National Defence terms of reference and the organization required for NORAD. The air officer commanding the R.C.A.F. air defence command at St. Hubert will continue to control all air defence operations over Canada.
The control of air defence over Canada depends in the first place on a requirement that all aircraft flying in Canadian air space must file a flight plan. The air defence authorities keep track of these flight plans, and by this method they are able to plot the movements of all aircraft flights in and out of and over Canada.
If the flight of an aircraft which does not coincide with a filed flight plan is picked up by any of the radar systems an investigation is immediately undertaken. If there are several aircraft this would, of course, be a serious matter and checks are immediately made with the United States strategic air force and other agencies operating large numbers of aircraft. The air defence system would automatically increase its state of readiness.
As soon as an unknown aircraft came within the range of our interceptor aircraft, investigation would be made in the air by these interceptors to ascertain the nature of the unknown aircraft. While this was going on Canadian and United States military authorities would be in contact so that the appropriate joint action could be taken if necessary. The air defence commanders would seek confirmation that these aircraft were in fact unscheduled flights. Other authorities would be giving consideration to the type of action to be taken by other forces and agencies. This would include, among other things, alerting the civil defence organization and ordering ships to sea.
I would point out to hon. members that the whole of this procedure is carried out in a matter of minutes. While these decisions are being taken the previously approved course of action by the air defence forces is under way. This is based on the rules of engagement which were approved by the government in December, 1951, and which define the powers and responsibilities of the air defence commander.
His powers are as follows. First, he may authorize the interception of aircraft in order to establish identification if other methods of obtaining identification have failed. Second, if the aircraft is identified as hostile by its appearance or because it perpetrates a hostile act or if its patent behaviour is sufficiently suspicious to justify a belief that it has hostile intentions, the air defence commander may authorize its engagement by fighters or other means. Third, if the aircraft

Supply-National Defence cannot be identified by any means whatever the air defence commander may, if circumstances warrant, authorize action to force the aircraft to land or engage it with fighters or other means.
These are the rules under which the R.C.A.F. air defence command has been operating since 1951, and it is these rules which will govern the activities of the air defence forces controlled by the commander in chief, North American air defence command. These rules are Canadian government policy; therefore the North American air defence command will be operating within approved government policy. Every country has established conditions and regulations similar to our rules of engagement under which aircraft can enter their air space. Such rules deal with aircraft which do not adhere to conditions of entry.
If military aircraft which are manifestly hostile in intent do enter Canadian territory without permission, an act of aggression has been committed against Canada and the use of force to deny these aircraft further passage over this country is an exercise of Canadian sovereignty and is not in itself an act which commits this country to war. Only the Canadian government can commit this country to war. Every precaution has been taken and will continue to be taken to ensure that the Canadian government is consulted before any act is undertaken which would commit this country to war.
The interception and destruction of enemy bombers over Canadian territory could not be construed as the initiation of aggression, because the presence of enemy bombers is in itself an act of aggression and consequently the air defence command is taking only protective measures. The interception and forcing down of aircraft which are invading our air space without permission, or destroying them when hostile intent is shown, is a national responsibility in the exercise of our sovereignty. Consequently the exercise of this authority under government approved procedures can safely be delegated to NORAD without fear that any defensive action taken would in itself initiate war. When the terms of reference and operating procedures for NORAD have been approved by both governments, the resulting exchange of notes will be tabled in this house.
I wish to consider now some other aspects of our defence planning and point out the part our regular and reserve forces are presently playing and will play in the future. To be effective the deterrent philosophy cannot depend on our retaliatory forces alone. It is as important that we should indicate to any would be aggressor that if necessary we


are prepared to fight on land, sea and in the air. If we do not indicate that we are prepared to fight should the deterrent fail, then this philosophy of the deterrent will also fail.
What kind of war must we be prepared to fight? With the introduction of nuclear weapons and the anticipated production of long-range ballistic missiles, it is obvious that the methods of waging any future war have clearly changed from those of world war II. Looking into the future is at best a risky business, but our military advisers must plan ahead, and it is their present opinion that a third world war would commence with a sudden ferocious thermonuclear attack of great intensity from several directions, by various means. Little or no warning could be expected; but this initial period, when the fight for survival would be paramount, is likely to decide the eventual outcome of the struggle. Therefore it is important at this stage that the forces required are trained, equipped and in position. There will be no time for mobilization or reinforcement because of the conditions expected to prevail in the first few days of a nuclear war.
It is considered that shipping and port facilities will not be available to dispatch large bodies of men and equipment to Europe in time to participate in the first phase of a war. Our dependence on forces in being therefore must be adhered to, and that is why we must continue to give top priority to our regular navy, army and air force. Only if we survive that initial stage of hostilities will it be possible to carry out additional military activities and, if necessary, raise and train additional forces.
With this in mind we must continually review our defence commitments and examine the means we have available to meet them within the limits of our economy. Defence costs now account for about one-third of the total federal budget, and there are those who may consider that reductions should be made. I will refer to those reductions later. By the elimination of overhead and duplication some money can be saved, but the fact remains that if we are to continue to play our part in the defence alliance we must see to it that our forces are equipped with modern weapons. These weapons, on account of their increasing complexity, are becoming more and more costly. I feel that in the world as it is today it would be folly to follow any other course than that we are now pursuing.

speechtext:
The knowledge that the Russians have a considerable number of long-range submarines perhaps capable of launching missiles far from our shores at targets well inland emphasizes the importance of the anti-submarine role of our navy, and presents new and serious problems. Fixed wing aircraft, helicopters and ships all have a part to play in detecting and destroying these submarines. Squadrons of the Tracker-a naval anti-submarine aircraft-are based on our new aircraft carrier Bonaventure. Seven of our new destroyer escorts are in commission, and another seven of the improved Resti-gouche class are nearing completion. Authority has also recently been given for the construction of two more of these outstanding ships.
Because the initiative will always rest with the enemy, it will be necessary for the navy to be operationally ready before any war begins, and to be in a position to deal with any submarine which might attempt to get within range of our Canadian ports. In this anti-submarine role our navy receives and works in close collaboration with the R.C.A.F. maritime command. As the Canadian built Argus aircraft comes into operation in this command the effectiveness of our seaboard defences will increase, and we are looking to the day when our naval and air force authorities will be able to keep track of and deal with all sea traffic above and below water in the same way that the air force keeps track of every aircraft in the sky over North America now.
If the R.C.A.F. is to continue to carry out its task efficiently it will have to improve its equipment constantly to cope with new aircraft flying at higher altitudes and at ever increasing speeds. That is why we are continuing the development of the CF-105, and that is why steps are being taken to evolve improved methods of processing information obtained through our warning systems, a complicated and very expensive proposition.
It is obvious-and this is indicated by changes taking place in the composition of the armies of the United Kingdom and the United States-that in an atomic age the Canadian regular army must strive for increased mobility and additional firepower. The strength of the regular army today is just under 49,000. We have in Europe the 4th Canadian infantry brigade group, to which I have already referred. In Canada 96698-121J
Supply-National Defence we have sufficient units to form three additional brigade groups, and it is our intention during the coming year to group these units so there will be a balanced brigade in western Canada, another brigade in central Canada, and a third in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces.
Each of these brigade groups will be commanded by a brigadier with an operational brigade staff. Each group will concentrate for summer training in Wainwright camp, in Petawawa or the Camp Borden-Meaford area, and at Gagetown. One battalion of each of these three brigade groups will have a parachute element and will be air-portable. The development of the Cariboo cargo aircraft by the deHavilland Company is proceeding satisfactorily, and steps are being taken to increase further our air transport capabilities.
The divisional headquarters as now organized will be reduced to nil strength during the next few months. Some divisional units will be retained, and the equipment for the headquarters will be kept available. The technique of command and administration will continue to be practised by general officers and their staffs so that if, at any future time, two or more of the brigade groups are operating together, personnel and equipment will be available to organize and operate a tactical divisional headquarters.
The launching of earth satellites and the reported successful firing of an intercontinental ballistic missile emphasize the need for the nations of the free world to collaborate in matters of defence, and point up the urgency of the pooling of scientific knowledge. Officials of the defence research board have for many years maintained close liaison with their opposite numbers in the United Kingdom and the United States. These fruitful discussions are now being intensified.
A major research contribution in support of the defence against the ICBM can be made by Canada in the field of radio propagation, particularly with reference to the auroral zone. This is being undertaken jointly with the United States air force at the Prince Albert radar site which is now in the course of construction.
Other programs now being undertaken by the defence research board are aimed at problems in the missile field, particularly with respect to ballistic detection; at means for countering submarines; at many phases of electronics in defence and at operational research studies designed to indicate the most economical means for obtaining maximum effectiveness from present and proposed weapons systems.

Supply-National Defence
The submarine threat is considered to be a grave one, and work in conjunction with the United States navy and the royal navy on improved anti-submarine detection devices is in progress. Projects are being undertaken with the objective of extending detection ranges and increasing the speed at which searches for submarines can be carried out. Studies of nuclear propulsion for ships are to be undertaken in conjunction with the royal navy, and a Canadian team of scientists and naval officers will proceed to the United Kingdom for this purpose early next year.
Our reliance on forces in being, to which I have already referred, will of necessity require some changes in the role of our reserve forces. The role of the naval reserve will remain the reinforcement of the fleet in being in time of emergency. Reserve personnel will also replace regular personnel ashore and will also be required to bring our ships up to war complement. Steps are being taken to ensure that the members of the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve will be immediately available and adequately trained for these duties. This rationalization will result in some reduction in present strength, because we are placing emphasis on quality rather than quantity.
Over the years the R.C.A.F. auxiliary squadrons have been an important element in our defence establishment. The first R.C.A.F. squadron to serve overseas in the second world war was an auxiliary squadron. The first fighter squadron was made up of 110 squadron from Toronto and 112 squadron from Winnipeg. These; squadrons are celebrating their 25th anniversary this year. Apart from the squadrons which saw service overseas, the auxiliary air force provided a large number of the trained personnel required to supervise and direct the activities of our expanding wartime air force. Since the war the auxiliary has continued to play an important role in the defence organization, and has assumed new tasks as and when required.
The changing tempo and technology of war have dictated an alteration in the role and employment of flying squadrons of our auxiliary air force. A careful reassessment of their role when viewed in the light of longterm requirements leads to an adjustment of effort which will enable the squadrons to contribute to the relief of civil emergency requirements in peace or war.
It has already been announced that certain squadrons are being equipped with light transport aircraft, and thus the first move was made toward the ultimate requirements for squadrons to be employed in an emergency
[Mr. Pearkes.l
and rescue role. There will continue to be a gradual change in other flying squadrons in the direction of this ultimate aim. As a step toward this goal, early next year the light bomber squadrons at Saskatoon and Edmonton will convert to this new role.
Also constituting a large portion of the R.C.A.F. auxiliary activities are the aircraft control and warning units. These units continue to play an important part and represent a readily available reserve of trained personnel for the support of the radar control stations in Canada. In this they are making a significant contribution to the air defence of this country.
Finally, the auxiliary technical training units which train technical personnel in support of the flying squadrons and the aircraft control and warning units will be adjusted in size in response to the gradual change proposed for the operational units which they support.
In so far as the militia are concerned, they have a long and brilliant record of achievement. Originally organized for the protection of the homes and lives of the very earliest settlers in this country, the members of the militia during the 18th and 19th centuries on many occasions, alone or in conjunction with British regulars, would indeed drive out the invader and give security to this country.
In 1914 and again in 1939, when our regular forces were very few in number, it was upon the units of the militia that we built our divisions for service overseas. Those who went overseas were in fact defending their homes and families, just as their forebears had done a century or more before; the same duties done and the same tasks performed, but some thousands of miles away.
Almost 20 years have passed since the outbreak of the second world war. Since then we have adopted a policy of having a large and efficient regular army of some 49,000 officers and men compared with approximately 4,000 in 1939. For the first time in history a potential aggressor, armed with new and modern weapons, including long-range air carriers, can make this continent a target for direct attack.
If, in spite of all our efforts, we are drawn into a major conflict, one of the first and vital battles may well be for survival within our own boundaries. The situation will be quite different from that which existed in 1914 and in 1939, when we had many months to mobilize and complete the training of tens of thousands of militiamen.
We anticipate two types of battle in which ground forces will be engaged. One battle

will be the direct contact with enemy ground forces in Europe, and will be fought by forces in being and in position. The other battle will be in this country, to assist in restoring order out of the terrible chaos that may result from enemy attacks with long range nuclear weapons. It is in this latter important battle that the militia as well as the regular and the civil defence organization will be needed.
The members of the militia must continue, however, to receive military training and retain a military organization, because it is this training and organization that make the militia so valuable in aiding the civil authorities. Many military skills are just the skills that are needed in all great disasters; for example, medical assistance and first aid, communications, engineering and repairs, traffic control and other such services.
War does not always follow the pattern one expects. It is quite conceivable that a situation may exist in which it will be of great value to have a reserve of at least partially trained personnel in all arms, who would be available as reinforcements. To meet our primary task in the battle for survival, the units of the militia will be grouped together into some 45 or 50 mobile columns. These columns will be trained to take their place in this battle, and will carry out exercises with local authorities and civil defence organizations.
I am well aware of the importance of our militia forces, and I am personally acquainted with the service our militia has performed in the past. They are a great body of public spirited citizens, and I have no doubt that they will carry out the vital role that is expected of them in the future.
I am pleased to state that enlistment into the militia and the strength of the militia are higher today than at any time previously this year.
I should like to make a few brief remarks regarding the 1957-58 estimates which are being presented to the committee. Since these estimates, amounting to $1,722,844,000, were prepared, increases in the rates of civil salaries and military pay and allowances have been authorized and took effect from May 1, 1957. The increases in military pay and allowances are estimated to amount to $27,574,892 for the 11 months of the fiscal year 1957-58 to which they apply, and the increases in civil salaries to $6,600,000 during the same period. There has, therefore, on this account been an extra amount of approximately $34,000,000. In addition, the cost of the mid-Canada line construction is expected to exceed the original estimate by
Supply-National Defence some $7 million. A supplementary estimate to cover these additions is not being requested, because a thorough review has been undertaken to make savings in other areas at least equal to this increase.
As a result of this review a number of decisions have been taken which will reduce expenditures. Savings are being made in the operating costs of all three services. A decision has been taken to discontinue the bureau of current affairs. Immediately on my taking office a review of advertising expenditures for recruiting purposes was made, and a reduction of these expenditures by one third was ordered. The curtailment of travelling expenses has also been directed; and while savings in the current year will not be large, in due course a helpful reduction may be expected in this field.
A detailed review of the construction program has been made and it has been possible to defer a number of lower priority items. The equipment programs have also been re-examined and some savings have been possible, notably the cancellation of the mark VI version of the CF-100 aircraft. A review is also continuing of those responsibilities of the defence department which might, with economy, be assumed by civilian departments of the government. One concrete result of these studies has been the decision to transfer the ice-breaker Labrador from the R.C.N. to the Department of Transport. Hon. members will recall the excellent work which this vessel did during the exploration of the Arctic this year.
It is now clear that these various savings will adequately take care of the additions caused by the salary increases. It is hoped that continued efforts will accomplish further savings before the close of the fiscal year. This will be done without affecting in any way the operational efficiency of our forces in being. It will be achieved by a reappraisal of planned projects and a readjustment of their priority in the light of the changing concept of military warfare.
In closing, I would point out to hon. members that the present fiscal year is now two-thirds over, and that a large percentage of the 1957-58 estimates are already spent. This, of course, in no way curtails the right of hon. members to raise any point they wish to make on this important subject of defence. I would suggest, however, that any general remarks should be included in the general debate, and that when we reach the estimates in detail we should discuss the items as set forth in the blue book.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking on the estimates of the Department of National Defence this afternoon I would first like to make a few comments on the statement delivered by the minister before the recess at noon. The courtesy which he extended to his predecessor, Hon. Ralph Campney-and I am sure he would extend the same courtesy to Hon. Brooke Claxton- was truly in keeping with the remarks I made on November 14, 1957, as reported at page 1151 of Hansard, with respect to the attitude of the minister in carrying out his responsibilities. He has today made only kind references to his predecessors.
I was also pleased to hear his remarks about the co-operation he has received from and the confidence he places in the senior officers of the armed services of this country. This is quite contrary to some of the remarks made on former occasions by some of his colleagues, particularly the Minister of Agriculture, who is presently in the committee.
In his remarks today I do not think the Minister of National Defence tried in any way to indicate to the committee or to the country that NORAD is a part of NATO, with which matter I will deal a little later, but he did say that the air defence scheme of the North American continent has been approved both by the government of Canada and the government of the United States. There might be some doubt about that when we refer to the evidence at the meeting of the committee on external affairs on December 2.
I thought I observed one discrepancy, though I might have misunderstood the minister, when he stated that there will be little that the NORAD commanders will be able to do in the first few hours of war except to reinforce the most threatened areas with whatever additional fighter aircraft and missiles become available after the battle is opened. I think this is directly opposed to the remarks made by the minister in a press release some time before this house opened, when he described the push-button control of the defence of the North American continent.
I was interested to note how the rules of aircraft flying over Canada apply and the requirements about filing flight plans and so on. This seems to contradict the reply of the minister in which he said that the whole procedure is carried out in a matter of
[Mr. Pearkes.l
moments. I submit that after flashing signals to the headquarters at Colorado Springs there will be no opportunity to spend some hours in preparation.
I was somewhat amazed at one statement made by the minister for which I am sure he must have an explanation, to the effect that the divisional headquarters as presently organized will be reduced in strength during the next few months. I presume he does not intend to leave us in the position where we would not be prepared for retaliatory ground action after an attack. He mentioned that there will be some reduction in the R.C.A.F. auxiliary squadrons, and it would seem important to remember that for the small cost involved in maintaining R.C.A.F. auxiliary squadrons they serve as a good pool of trained personnel to keep available in case we wish to expand our use of retaliatory armed bombers.
In the statement he made this morning concerning the reduction of the ground forces it appeared that the minister disregarded the possibility of further local skirmishes or infiltration by an enemy into this country, and that he has not made adequate provision for preventing such happenings by having trained forces available in reserve. On such occasions it may very well be that the regular forces, which in the future will be composed of trained technicians, will have their hands full in dealing with matters of a more technical nature than would be required in the case of skirmishes or infiltration.
I listened with interest to the minister's explanation of the present role of the militia and the role it will adopt in future. I notice that he included in his explanation a comment to the effect that the militia would also take military training along with the civil defence training, which he stated on previous occasions would be emphasized. Under the schedule of training of the militia in the past it took two years to produce a trained soldier. I had an opportunity to review a directive concerning training as it will be conducted, and taking into account the same amount of training it will be spread over a period of five years. In other words it will take five years to produce a trained soldier for the reserve if the new directive for training is carried out. There is a turnover of men in the militia approximately every two years, and it occurred to me that under the new schedule of training there would be a very low percentage of trained personnel, as far as military training is concerned, if the new trend in the training of militia is to continue.
In the minister's statement I observed no mention of waste and extravagance in his

department, and I am sure he will agree with us that before he took over there had been a paring down to the basic essentials.
In relation to construction and the requirements of equipment the minister mentioned that there was a deferment. It seems to me that when there is a deferment we just put off from this year to next year those things we might have needed this year. The construction and requirements of equipment for this year are essential to the welfare of the country, and in particular it would assist the employment situation if such construction were allowed to progress during this winter.
I realize that my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence was for many years a great soldier; and today a great soldier, for several years the defence critic of the official opposition in this house, now finds himself in a new position. He is on the pinnacle where he must initiate a policy to defend Canada, one that would prepare us to retaliate and destroy an aggressor. The position, I am sure, must feel new to him, but he is not alone in this situation because our great partner to the south, the United States, also has a new secretary of defence with but nine weeks of experience on the job. This is all the more reason why particular care must be taken to formulate a defence policy in accordance with the present circumstances, events and eventualities.
We had expected that today Canada's new defence minister would have made a more detailed reappraisal of the defence of Canada, if we were to read and expect action from the speeches he has made in the past. I was disappointed the other day when a member of the C.C.F. party asked about a white paper and received a negative reply. It would seem to me that this would have been the appropriate time when, as the minister explained, there had not only been a change in personnel of the government but a great change in the weapons of war, for the minister to have made available a reappraisal and an assessment of the problem in a white paper.
He has made very little available as far as a report of his appraisal of the defence of Canada is concerned. We know that scientific developments and announcements within the last month do justify a reappraisal of our defences, a report to the nation on our defences, and an assurance from the Minister of National Defence or the Prime Minister that scientific research with respect to defence weapons is progressing.
I do not think it is essential that we must always, in this instance anyway, follow the footsteps of our neighbour to the south. There is an underlying uneasy feeling that the United States has become inferior in some
Supply-National Defence respects compared with Russia. If our government feels that certain items of defence are lagging owing to United States tardiness we must be prepared to take the lead as we did in the Suez question, or encourage the United States to speed up.
My hon. friend the Minister of National Defence, and his government, I must say are faced with some problems right now, and one of the biggest problems is the defence of this country. Even with the use of conventional, outmoded weapons, their first problem is manpower, but manpower now required in addition to the conventional troops who still may be required in the category of manpower which I have indicated. How is the minister recruiting and keeping civilian scientists and engineers? Are his service personnel becoming the skilled technicians, or in other words has he sufficient brain power, in the light of recent weapon advances, in his military establishments? I am sure the minister would want to report to us and assure us that we are not lagging in that department.
We are also dependent upon Canadian industry and the industry of other nations for the weapons of war. The minister should tell us what effort he has made to have industry in Canada continue to co-operate with our defence program as it did in world war II, when Right Hon. C. D. Howe headed the department of munitions and supply. I would not like to feel that our industry has been discouraged in morale and frustrated by the lack of a fiscal and trade policy.
It has been reported that there have been interservice rivalries, and that there has been some waste in defence funds and a slowdown in the development of new weapons. I am sure the minister should report to us to erase this inference. The minister would also want to assure us, since the militia has been more or less erased, that we shall have sufficient conventional troops to discourage a conventional attack or a mop-up after a conventional attack upon our country. We are entitled to know whether under the policy of the government he intends to scrap the development and production of manned planes in favour of an accelerated missile program.
The minister, in formulating his policy, must consider whether he wishes to put greater dependence on nuclear air power and reduction in conventional forces, to the point where his policy has led to an inflexible situation by which we could not meet a threat *of local limited war.
I notice that in his statement this morning the minister was more or less of the opinion that if we had an attack it would be an allout attack. It seems to me that there are two types of nuclear war, a total one and a limited one. Some think of a nuclear conflict only in

Supply-National Defence terms of mushroom clouds, total devastation over vast areas and an all-out nuclear war. This might never come about, because it might be disastrous to both sides.
The scientists today are concentrating on nuclear weapons which can pinpoint their effort without radiation; for instance, a weapon which could be pinpointed upon a troop or civilian concentration. These weapons could be used in a limited nuclear war, limited in scope, in arms and in area and waged by professional fighting men. This type of war could be triggered or push-buttoned if and when an aggressor should attack North America. This type of war would be a distinct possibility. Nuclear war would be short, including the detonation and mopping up. It would be over in days or possibly in weeks.
The new nuclear weapons and the H-bomb have provided this nation and other nations of the world that may be involved in a war with a great many avenues of thought and policy. There are those who say that if we find ourselves in war we should use our most effective weapons against our enemies. Today the most effective weapons which warring nations would have would be the H-bomb and nuclearweapons. If we can believe reports from the United States-whatever the truth is of the Russian claim to having successfully tested an intercontinental ballistic missile-they are ahead of the Russians. If this is so it is an immense advantage to Canada as well as to other NATO nations, but we must bear in mind the fact that there is a great possibility that nuclear war would be a limited one. There would then, as the minister told us this morning, be no time to mobilize and train troops and engineer and produce weapons, process and store the essentials of life, food, and so on. This is an important matter. If we are to win this type of war we must win it years ahead by preparedness.
The minister mentioned NORAD this morning. I should like to refer for a few moments to sessional paper No. 183, which contains the order in council dated July 31, 1957, along with a joint statement by the secretary of defence of the United States and the Minister of National Defence of Canada. I might say that I agree with the policy of the joint air defence of North America. Among other things, I was interested in the principles and procedures which are involved in the establishment of this particular defence. I think it needs a review and some scrutiny. I am assured that this is the only document that deals with the important matter of this particular phase of the defence of North America. Yesterday when I asked the Minister of National Defence whether there was any further order in council dealing with this matter

other than the one to which I have referred, his answer was in the negative.
For a moment I should like to put on the record what I really think this order in council does. As I see it, it does two things. It appoints Air Marshal Slemon and makes provision for his pay. It instructs him that he is to take his orders from a superior at the Colorado headquarters. There is something else that has been raised. What justifies the 40 members of his staff being out of this country under a foreign commander, General Partridge? I do not believe we have had that answered yet in this house, except probably by an explanation which added to the confusion.

It is now some time Since the order in council was passed, and we have been advised that over this period of time there has been consultation, but we have found that there has been consultation on a military level only. Included in the statement issued by the secretary of defence of the United States and the Minister of National Defence of Canada, which statement accompanied the order in council, there is a particular sentence which is important and which I should like to read. It is in these words:
This system of integrated operational control and the setting up of a joint headquarters will become effective at an early date.
That was five months ago. The statement that the command became operative immediately is further supported by the answer to a question I asked the Minister of National Defence on November 5, as found at pages

757 and 758 of Hansard. I asked the minister if the command was operative, and the minister replied:
Yes, it is operative on an interim basis until the formal agreement has been drawn up as I explained to the house.
Hon. members will realize that an agreement must have some limitations, and although we might agree with the policy or purpose of the order in council we certainly would like to know what the limitations and details of the agreement are at this time, five months after some kind of an arrangement was made, during which period of time the headquarters of General Partridge and Air Marshal Slemon has been operative.
We were particularly interested in knowing what consultation there had been with the government of Canada, and on November 6, 1957 I asked the minister how there could be consultation with the government of Canada prior to Canadian fighters being put in the air if there was an attack by an aggressor. The minister answered, "Mr. Speaker, by telephone or other means." On that same day there was the following exchange between the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Essex East as found at page 812 of Hansard:

It certainly is.
The Prime Minister agreed that it was extremely important. In the light of the meeting of the external affairs committee the other day and in the light of what has been said in the house and the reference in the minister's statement this morning, it would seem that the same principles were involved as in the case of the arrangement made in the early part of world war II by Mr. King and Mr. Roosevelt. For the sake of clarification perhaps I might read a portion of Mr. King's speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne at the 1940-41 session of parliament. I wish to refer to page 54 of Hansard for November 12, 1940.
Perhaps I might preface what I am about to read by saying that even at this stage, five months after the arrangement was made for NORAD, the Department of External Affairs has never been consulted with respect to any agreement or arrangement with the United States concerning the defence of the North American continent and the involvement of Canada in that defence. I will refer to that later, as that was one of the matters
Supply-National Defence discussed by the external affairs committee earlier this week. Mr. King had this to say in his address:
The first inkling of developments already under way was given to the public by the President of the United States, on August 16. On that day Mr. Roosevelt announced that:
"The United States government is holding conversations with the government of the British Empire with regard to acquisition of naval and air bases for the defence of the western hemisphere and especially the Panama canal. The United States government is carrying on conversations with the Canadian government on the defence of the western hemisphere."
I shall have something to say to the house in a moment about these conversations. I wish first to recall the events which followed immediately on President Roosevelt's announcement.
The following day, which was August 17, I met the president at Ogdensburg. Our conversations that day, in continuance of conversations previously held, culminated in the formulation of an agreement which was made public the next afternoon, in a joint statement issued by Mr. Roosevelt and myself.	[DOT]
I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that in this instance the early stages had passed, the command now became or was immediately operative, and the matter was not dealt with on a military level but a government level, which I suggest is a complete difference in principle from what has been applied in the case of NORAD.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON POLICY RESPECTING SATELLITE STATIONS
speechtext: There is quite a difference now, too. There was a war on then.

speechtext:
Well, there is more time to make an agreement now and probably reach an agreement much faster without having other things to do. The Prime Minister and the president had discussed the mutual problems, and these were the terms of the agreement:
The Prime Minister and the President have discussed the mutual problems of defence in relation to the safety of Canada and the United States.
It has been agreed that a permanent joint board on defence shall be set up at once by the two countries.
This permanent joint board on defence shall commence immediate studies relating to sea, land and air problems including personnel and material.
It will consider in the broad sense the defence of the north half of the western hemisphere.
The permanent joint board on defence will consist of four or five members from each country, most of them from the services. It will meet shortly.
It is interesting to note that the instance which concerns us at the present time, NORAD, does not conform to the same principles that were adopted at the beginning of world war II. As found on page 56, Mr. King stated:
Our common problems of defence were discussed at length and in a more concrete and definite way when I visited Washington in November, 1938, to sign the new Canadian-United States trade agreement.

Supply-National Defence
I think it is interesting to place on record the minute of cabinet in 1940, which is not included in sessional paper 183 to which I referred today. On page 56 there is also the following:
By a minute of council approved by His Excellency the Governor General on August 21, the establishment of the permanent joint board on defence was formally ratified and confirmed.
With the permission of the house, I should like to insert in Hansard a copy of the complete minute.
The copy of the complete minute sets out very well the procedure to be followed in the establishment of a joint command of this nature. It is in these terms:
The committee of the privy council had had before them a report, dated August 20, 1940, from the Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs, representing:
That on August 17, 1940, at the invitation of the President of the United States, he proceeded to the United States to Ogdensburg in the state of New York, to meet Mr. Roosevelt for the purpose of discussing mutual problems of defence in relation to the safety of Canada and the United States.
If I may stop there for a moment, we can see that this arrangement certainly was on a political level and not a military level, as was indicated in the external affairs committee this week. I continue with the following quotation found in the minute:
The Prime Minister and the President have discussed the mutual problems of defence in relation to the safety of Canada and the United States.
It has been agreed that a permanent joint board on defence shall be set up at once by the two countries.
This permanent joint board on defence shall commence immediate studies relating to sea, land and air problems, including personnel and material.
It will consider in the broad sense the defence of the north half of the western hemisphere.
The permanent joint board on defence will consist of four or five members from each country, most of them from the services. It will meet shortly.
That the actions of the Prime Minister in conducting the said conversations and in agreeing, on the part of Canada, to the establishment of a permanent joint board on defence for the consideration of the defence of the north half of the western hemisphere, are in accord with the policy of the government as approved on many occasions by the war committee of the cabinet and the cabinet itself.
May I state, Mr. Chairman, that in the instances we have been discussing this session we have had no indication from the present government on this matter, although they would like to say that this matter was discussed in cabinet and that it received the approval of the war committee of the cabinet; I presume that today that would be called the defence committee of the cabinet.
The Prime Minister, therefore, recommends that his actions in conducting the said conversations and in agreeing to the establishment of the said permanent joint board on defence be ratified and confirmed.

The committee concur in the foregoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
I might say that beyond page 57 Mr. King also related that these declarations marked the first public recognition by both countries of reciprocity in defence.
In the sessional paper we had filed, and the order in council with the statement of the Minister of National Defence and of the secretary of defence for the United States, we failed to have a cabinet minute.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. If I may, I should like to direct my remarks for a moment to the manner in which the principle involved in the establishing of NORAD has been handled. May I make an observation from the committee on external affairs, where the Secretary of State for External Affairs was asked what relationship there is, if any, between Canada's participation or membership in NATO and the joint air defence program with the United States. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said he was unable to answer that question. He was then asked where he could get the answer.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, I observe, was prepared to make a statement about NORAD; and he said the Prime Minister had made a statement in the house, and that this question would be considered further on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. He reiterated with emphasis that so far as his department are concerned they had not been brought into this matter whatsoever, that there had been a discussion on the military level and that his department would deal with the political aspect of it.
It seems to me at this time that although the command is operative, this matter never reached the level of the political aspect, nor has parliament been advised or been able to approve of any permanent or fixed formal agreement which there might be between the two countries with respect to the air defence of North America. It would seem that the principles involved in making an arrangement of this kind between the two countries are not in any way similar to the principles involved in the procedure as between Mr. Roosevelt and Mr. King in 1940.

If I might just bring my remarks to a conclusion at this time, I should like to do so by saying this. The other night I was reading the Dulles policy as outlined by Mr. James Shepley in Life magazine January 16th, 1956, in an article entitled "How Dulles Averted War Three Times-He Brought U.S. Back From the Brink". I should like to conclude these remarks with a sort of warning to the present Minister of National Defence and the present Secretary of State for External Affairs that they should review the situation and make sure that in the handling of a matter so important as NORAD, the joint air defence of North America by Canada and the United States, they have not conducted matters so loosely that there would be a possibility that they might be involved in a policy of what we might call this "brinkmanship"; that Canada by inadvertence, lack of information, negligence, carelessness or otherwise, might unnecessarily be brought into a sphere of policy whereby war would be thrust upon us not of our own making or concurrence.

speechtext:
I was very happy to listen to the minister this morning when introducing for the first time his estimates to this house. We sat in very close proximity in the last house and were often able to have a chat. I have a very high regard for him, but I must say that I do not envy him in the task that lies before him in this extremely important department.
When I was participating in the external affairs debate on November 26 I stated that we should take a new look at our external policies as well as those of national defence, because the two departments and their policies are more or less linked closely together. Today the Minister of National Defence has introduced estimates that were compiled by his predecessor in office and before some very startling new developments occurred in the production of nuclear and thermonuclear weapons in the past six months.
May I say to my friend the hon. member for Kingston that I do not see that it is realistic at all to talk about a limited nuclear war. I do not believe that such a thing is possible. It seems to us that these estimates are not only sadly out of date but that they should be carefully scrutinized by this parliament before they are approved and adopted. I recollect how hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were in opposition, demanded that the estimates of the Department of National Defence presented by the former Liberal administration should be scrutinized by a committee of the House of Commons. What they said then I think is true today, and even
Supply-National Defence more true than it was then. On June 21, 1956, as reported at page 5244 of Hansard of that year the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Drew, had this to say:
The estimates now before us call for an expenditure of $1,775 million.
That is almost identical with the amount we are discussing today.
Further amounts probably will be added by the supplementary estimates which will be presented later. What have we before us to really tell us whether this money is being properly spent or otherwise? We really have nothing but bland assurances which were not substantiated by the detailed facts which would make it possible for us to pass judgment on this vitally important question.
I say that what Mr. Drew had to say on that date is equally applicable this afternoon. We have nothing but bland assurances with no facts to make it possible for us to pass judgment on this vitally important question. We have not even a new white paper. The white paper we have before us is the one that was presented to this house by the former minister of national defence last April. If I may quote again I should like to do so. Speaking in the same debate on June 22, 1956, the present Prime Minister said this, as reported at page 5321 of Hansard:
We are left in the dark. We do not know. In order to obtain information we have to read the reports of the United States Senate committee or the House of Representatives committee . . . Are we receiving value for our expenditures? One does not have to have the knowledge gained by committees to conclude that in too large a measure there has been a wasteful disregard of the requirements of the people as a whole and waste of the moneys collected from the people through taxation.
Even today we are obliged to learn a great deal about North American defence from representations and statements, of which I will perhaps say more in a moment, that are made before a committee of the Senate of the United States. Today we are left more in the dark than ever before, because apparently the Minister of National Defence, without any conference with the Department of External Affairs, has committed our armed forces in North America to the control of a United States commander without the safeguards which we insisted upon when, through diplomatic channels, we agreed to place certain of our forces under the North Atlantic treaty command or, as my hon. friend said a few moments ago, following the Ogdensburg conversations between Mr. King and the late President Roosevelt.
When were these arrangements reached? We do not know. As the hon. gentleman a few moments ago pointed out, we have just the one document, the order in council, and a press statement; that is all we know about it. If the rumours are correct this had
1910	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence been before the former government for some time, on the recommendation of the former minister, but the former government felt it could not approve of the arrangement; yet this decision was made shortly after the present government took office, on July 31 this year. How was it done? Where was it done? And what assurances were given prior to the passing of this order in council? Perhaps we shall get that a little later on. We certainly should.
One could quote extensively from speeches made by the new cabinet ministers including the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of National Defence himself, to the effect that these estimates should be more carefully scrutinized by a parliamentary committee than they have been, and today we have nothing further to substantiate the defence estimates than we had in previous years.
As I said a few moments ago, in the past few months fantastic changes have taken place in the world's military technology, accompanied by almost as rapid changes in strategy and tactics. Indeed, progress in current military science has become so accelerated that nearly every weapon now designed is said to be a transitional weapon soon to be superseded by something more revolutionary. The staggering increase in the rate of obsolescence of weapons of war is a problem which not only all military planners must face but which parliaments like our own must consider before we agree to stupendous expenditures without careful inquiry into the validity of the demands of this department.
We must also ask ourselves today to what extent is it wise or possible to continue to adhere to an arms race when we know that the new and terrible weapons of war give neither security to our people nor defence. Air force General Earl E. Partridge, commander in chief of NORAD, to whom our own Canadian defences have been committed, asserted before a Senate committee-I might say before Russia had launched her satellite- as follows:
If the aggressor's weapon is the intercontinental ballistic missile this continent stands today almost as naked as it did in 19.46, for I have no radar to detect missiles and no defence against them.
This statement is one we should bear in mind when we are considering the recommendations now before us from the Department of National Defence. While these are the estimates for 1957 to 1958-and one does not care to move any reduction in them because much of the money has already been spent-if estimates different from these are not brought in for 1958-59, then I think some


of us will have to move for a reduction in the estimates, particularly if no parliamentary committee is set up to inquire very carefully into these matters at that time.
As I said in the external affairs debate, the only defence possible is one based upon the elimination of war itself through negotiation with other countries-particularly those who may be potential aggressors. Yesterday again one of the military leaders of the United States was reported as having said-and I heard this myself, of course, over the C.B.C.- that the Russians were so far ahead of the United States that there was imminent danger of destruction. His solution, of course, was that more money and more energy must be devoted to more weapons for United States armies and those of her allies. There was no suggestion that a new approach must be taken to end the disastrous arms race which is now in full effect-with Russia, I might add, apparently in the lead.
In the circumstances now clear to us all, we have lost the power to defend ourselves. Nor have the Russians power to defend their people in their country, for General Norstad, head of NATO, testified before his Senate committee a few weeks ago that the west could attack Russia from 250 NATO bases in a complete circle around that country, and that even if the Soviets had 200 per cent of his attacking power they would still be destroyed. Incidentally, when we were given this information we were told it was confidential, but before the senate committee of the United States General Norstad makes this statement publicly and openly, and it is reported in the United States press. Apparently the United States Senate can be given information which is denied to us except under confidential or secret circumstances.
It is a grim situation which faces us when we begin to examine the proposals and expenditures of the Department of National Defence, yet our leaders continue to talk in terms of war. I said in the debate on external affairs that the present arms race really dates from the production of the atomic bomb in 1945. It was then that one of the wisest United States statesmen, Mr. Stinson, secretary of the army during the second world war, told the last United States cabinet meeting which he attended in September, 1945, that "unless the Soviets are voluntarily invited into partnership upon a basis of cooperation and trust" a desperate arms race would follow. Mr. Stinson urged direct negotiations with Russia to that end, and at once, but unfortunately his advice was not followed.
Similar sentiments were expressed in the United Kingdom and in Canada, but

Supply-National Defence
Washington decided to keep the atomic bomb, as she called it, "a sacred trust". So, on November 15, 1945, the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada issued a declaration which did the very thing that Stinson had warned against. Since then we ourselves have spent many billions of dollars on defence. Indeed, nearly one-third of our entire budget in recent years has been spent in this field, or one-half of our controllable expenditures.
The estimates now before us provide for an expenditure of $1,717, million and these may have to be supplemented before the end of the current year, I do not know.
