I am glad to hear the minister say that. We are warned that if we proceed to reorient our military requirements in the direction of modern nuclear and thermonuclear weapons this amount will have to be vastly increased as the years go by.
What is the alternative? On October 7 the New York Times, which has given consistent support to United States leadership in the cold war and against Russia and the satellite countries, had this to say:
The truth is at once more ominous, more exacting and more enchanting. The greatest adventure of ail is not to go to the moon or to explore the rings of Saturn. It is rather to understand the heart and soul of man and to turn away from wrath and destruction and toward creativeness and brotherly love. We cannot look at the world today without realizing that our mastery of ourselves has not kept pace with our mastery of inanimate nature. We now have the power to destroy each other and all the works of civilization, but we have not yet invented a sure way to control this power. In a sense, a part of us never came down from the tree, never crawled out of the cave. Now we must arise out of our long childhood and play the part of wise, mature and humane men-all of us, all mankind, of whatever political or religious faith-or we shall surely die.
This is a very different statement to the kind of statement which comes under the description of the "brinkmanship" of Mr. John Foster Dulles. There is no doubt that the idea of defence is regarded by many people as a principal function of the national state. Yet today we know there is not a people on the face of the earth who can be defended from wholesale and terrible death and destruction if another big war comes. Obviously then we are on the brink of destruction, with no sure defence, unless we revise our national policies and rely on negotiation instead of piling up obsolete weapons of war for which we are providing again in the estimates now before us.
As I said at the outset, our defence program, in spite of the change in government, is to continue free from adequate inquiry under the critical scrutiny of a parliamentary
committee. Unlike the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States, the Canadian government has never been compelled to justify before parliament its defence policy involving huge annual expenditures. We should now demand that it do so.
Yet these expenditures, to a very large extent indeed, are for the production and maintenance of obsolete weapons that could contribute little or nothing to the defence of Canada. One could go into each branch of the services and show how pitifully inadequate they are to meet the threat of modern nuclear war. We are still spending huge sums of money on conventional weapons that, by comparison, are as out of date as the weapons used in the South African war were out of date in the second world war.
Our air force, which like our other services contains well-trained and devoted personnel, is equipped with planes that, we are told by competent authorities, are now quite obsolete. Both the United States and the U.S.S.R. have modern planes which are far in advance of anything we possess; yet they too offer no defence against the guided missile. Even before the recent and startling developments Lieutenant General Guy Simonds, the retired chief of our army general staff, on the C.B.C. television program "Citizens' Forum", last February declared that the re-equipping of the R.C.A.F. home squadrons with the mark V of the CF-100 was money "down the drain" since the plane was already obsolete.
Those are not my words. They are the words of Lieutenant General Guy Simonds. Is it true that the conversion of our air force to the mark V CF-105 would cost about $8 million per unit or over $1 billion in all? All this would be required to convert one obsolete plane into another obsolete plane, if we may take what Lieutenant General Guy Simonds says as an accurate statement of the position.
One could develop this statement still further and point out that apart altogether from the guided missiles, these obsolete planes could never intercept the higherflying and faster Soviet intercontinental jet bombers if they were loosed upon us. Nor, as General Partridge has already indicated, can the three radar screens, namely the "Pine-tree" line, near the Canada-United States border, the mid-Canada line, or the distant early warning line, apprise our cities or our forces of the approach of the new intercontinental ballistic missiles.
And into all this we are pouring hundreds of millions of dollars. In an article in Macleans magazine of February 18, 1956- and again, may I say, before the Russians announced the success of their intercontinental ballistic missile-General Macklin,

Supply-National Defence who was adjutant general of the Canadian army until last June wrote:
This being a free country, it is open to the advocates and architects of this gigantic defence to justify its terrific cost in money, machinery and men to the groaning taxpayers who have to pay for it. I am not aware that, so far, they have made any notable efforts to do so.
The whole business has been announced to parliament and the public bit by bit and many of the details are still hidden from us. Perhaps they have to be, in the interests of security, though "security" has far too often itself been used as a wall behind which many an expensive bonehead play has passed unseen by the public.
And we know perfectly well that we have been told in this house on former occasions by former ministers of defence that some of the equipment, orders for which were placed in the factories at the blueprint stage, would be obsolete before the actual equipment came off the line. I believe I remember Mr. Brooke Claxton telling us that in this house with regard to some aircraft.
Members of the house are, therefore, entitled to ask the new government of Canada to justify these estimates which were placed before us by the previous administration and which are quite similar to those which from time to time the gentlemen who now occupy the posts of responsibility, vacated by the Liberals, criticized so severely. We have no right to pass these estimates without the most careful inquiry and scrutiny.
However, from what I have said it is obvious that we believe there is no hope of defence in the proposals that are now before us. On the contrary, we believe that Canada must press for a new look at our defence and international policies which are so inextricably linked. We believe that our surest defence lies in endeavouring to bring about a progressive reduction in defence expenditures through the elimination of threats of war. Hence we urge our government to use its influence to further the cause of world peace through negotiation. We believe that if these estimates were thoroughly investigated and all expenditures for obsolete planes and obsolete equipment of every description eliminated, we could transfer substantial sums of money for the most effective means of human well-being and international security.
The future of the world is not going to be decided on the battlefields, because battlefields may make the future of mankind uncertain. On the contrary, the devotion of our efforts to the relief of human suffering, the promotion of human health, and relief of world-wide hunger would do more to promote world peace and our own security than any other endeavour we could undertake. I should
[Mr. Coldwell.l
like to repeat a quotation from the editorial of the New York Times to which I have already referred:
Now we must arise out of our long childhood and play the part of wise, mature and humane men- all of us, all mankind, of whatever political or religious faith-or we shall surely die.
Unfortunately the signs are few that governments will take effective steps to ensure that we have peace unless they are forced to do so by a mighty demand from the peoples whom they govern. Only an aroused and awakened public opinion can stop this drive to universal annihilation, and as far as we are concerned in this house with the estimates before us, can we say to the people of Canada that after we have spent every penny of this $1,717 million Canada is going to be any safer for it, when we know, and are told by competent authorities such as the three I have named, that we have no assurance of warning in case of attack, that the equipment we are relying upon for defence is obsolete, and that we have been spending hundreds of millions of dollars wastefully?
I say to the new government that I am surprised that after all they said when in opposition regarding the need for a scrutiny of these estimates they should come before us with these estimates practically unchanged and ask us to vote them virtually in toto. We expected that they would set up a committee early this session before which we could call the responsible officials of the department for questioning regarding these expenditures.
Right from the conclusion of the last war the door has been shut against members of parliament inquiring into the activities of this department. We have been told that national security demanded it. But in the light of statements which are now being made by General Partridge, and the fact that our own air force is under the control, as I understand it, of a foreign government these estimates should be scrutinized. The hon. gentleman is shaking his head. He has been shaking his head all afternoon-I do not mean the minister but the hon. gentleman beside him, probably his assistant. He can shake his head as much as he likes, but that will not stop me from saying what I think, and not only what I think and wish to place before the house, but what some other people more competent to judge than he is seem to think.
I want to conclude my remarks by saying that this parliament owes a duty to this country not to let these estimates pass lightly but to see to it that we look into matters carefully, make up our minds what we should do about it, stop the waste and inefficiency and

the obsolescence in this department and co-operate with all others as far as we can to achieve the only way in which mankind can find safety, by the removal of the threat of nuclear war from this country and the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I begin by admitting that I do not pose as a military expert. I am speaking strictly as a layman who would like to see the right thing but perhaps not knowing exactly what the right thing would be in the field of armaments and military science. I would say at the outset that we deeply appreciate the courtesy of the minister not only today but since he came into his important office because on a number of occasions this year the present minister has given evidence of a desire to keep us informed and help us understand the rather difficult problems that arise from time to time. I want also to express to him our thanks for his courtesy in sending us a copy of his speech which he delivered earlier today. This thoughtful action gave me a better opportunity to follow exactly what he had in mind with regard to government policy.
If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and I had got together earlier today or yesterday I do not suppose we could have followed a more parallel course in what we have to say. I should like to begin by discussing the matter of the committee which he brought up and there is only one thing I can say that would differ from what he has presented here as a good reasoned argument for the committee. I gave him and his colleagues a chance just the other day to make it possible for us to have a committee of that kind set up and he and his colleagues turned down the proposal by voting against the amendment we moved.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON POLICY RESPECTING SATELLITE STATIONS
speechtext:
Otherwise we will never have the careful scrutiny of these estimates which he suggested we must have. We, too, feel that recent developments in the field of intercontinental ballistic missiles and interspace travel and advances in all branches of technology require a reappraisal of our whole defence policy. We feel that such a reappraisal must not be left exclusively to the
Supply-National Defence military leaders of this country. This parliament must apply itself diligently to this particular task, too. Neither the time nor the facilities are available in the committee of the whole in which we find ourselves at this moment to do what anybody could possibly call an efficient job.
The government should have set up a defence estimates committee early in the present session to get started with its work and that work should be carried on continually for the duration of this parliament. Nothing less than many months of effort would be required to secure the information which we should have if the reappraisal I spoke of is to be made.
We suggest that this committee should have the authority to summon witnesses and send for papers. I suggest to the minister that it is not too late yet. We cannot in conscience do less than our full duty as representatives of the people and I say we are not doing our full duty unless we make a very careful and detailed scrutiny of the proposed estimates for defence. The establishment of a committee to study the estimates in the greatest detail is essential if any worth-while reappraisal of our defence policy is to be made.
Such a committee is especially essential in the light of the foolish policy the government has adopted in trying to force unduly the present session to a conclusion. The other day I said what I deeply feel in that connection. I cannot possibly see how anybody could declare that he has done his full duty to the people who sent him here and to his country if he does not prepare himself to stay here as long as it is necessary to thoroughly scrutinize the estimates, particularly those of the Department of National Defence, and study and reappraise our whole defence policy. That is one of the reasons I feel, as I said the other day, it is foolhardy to suggest we should start sitting longer hours for the purpose of trying to finish up before Christmas or perhaps just a few days after Christmas. It seems utterly childish and foolish to me to make this attempt and in all seriousness I suggest that the government even yet should reconsider its determined policy in this regard and agree to the setting up of the committee about which we have spoken.
I would like to mention that earlier this year on February 26, 1957, when the leader of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Quebec East who was then prime minister moved a motion to appoint a select committee on estimates, the hon. gentleman who is now the Prime Minister had some rather cogent remarks to make and I would like to quote

Supply-National Defence his comments as they appear at page 1655 and the following pages of Hansard. This is what the present Prime Minister had to say on that occasion as reported at page 1655:
Today expenditures are fabulous in amount and, except for ministers in the government, there are no adequate research opportunities whereby parliament may properly discharge its responsibilities.
This was part of the hon. gentleman's argument for a better opportunity for members of this house to study the detailed estimates and secure information from the department so they would know what they were doing.
The hon. gentleman who is now the Prime Minister, as reported at page 1657, had this to say:
Throughout the years I have said-and I repeat it now-
You notice that he admits having said it throughout the years which would indicate it was a conviction with him and if it was a conviction with him through those years I suggest it should be now. I continue:
Throughout the years I have said-and I repeat it now-that there is today no means whereby expenditures can be examined. There is no means available. In the first place, members of the opposition naturally have not that research knowledge which is necessary; they have not available to them the civil service. They are obliged to depend on information that comes in that desultory way that has existed throughout the years. Gladstone once said:	It is more difficult
to save a shilling than to spend a million. An estimates committee, properly set up, could bring about savings in this country which would be beneficial not only to the departments concerned but above all to the taxpayers.
Up to the present time, with the exception of that committee which was set up during the days of the war-I refer to the war expenditures committee-there has been no serious endeavour through the years to meet this problem of a careful examination and scrutiny coupled with the necessary recommendations as to the achievement of savings.
I agree with that and I believe the argument is just as valid today as it was on February 26 or at any previous time for the setting up of a committee for the purpose of a detailed analysis of the estimates of which we are about to go into as careful a study as is allowed in the committee of the whole in the few remaining days left before the government hopes to adjourn or prorogue or whatever it is going to do.
Then the hon. gentleman said this:
The committee that is now being set up- Which was the committee on estimates-
-under this resolution is but a copy of the one that has been in existence for two years. In the light of that experience I say that unless it has the power to call witnesses and to ask for papers, it is nothing but a sham and a delusion.
Well, what is the use of having a committee unless you do clothe it with the authority to

call witnesses and to ask for papers? It would be a sham and a delusion. Therefore, the committee we are asking for should be clothed with the authority to call witnesses, especially, Mr. Chairman, in the light of the fact that over these past few months we have retired generals of the army who have made scathing criticisms of the way in which our defence policy is being applied. But I do not necessarily believe all that General Simonds has said, nor General Macklin, both of whom were quoted by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar; but the very fact that those people were in the know, that those people had great responsibility while they were leaders of our military forces in this country, gives some credence to what they say. It seems to me that in the light of what General Simonds said particularly, as is quoted in the Ottawa Citizen of November 6, 1957, we should have a committee. By the way what he said was headlined in these words:
Millions Wasted on Obsolete Arms, Simonds Attacks Suicidal Policy
He goes on to make some pretty strong accusations, and he says at one point that he saw only marginal hope that the defence department will modify its policies. He is speaking of the new one. He continues:
"They spend too much time trying to think up defences for their past decisions, justifying past policies."
Much of the trouble, he said, stemmed from "vested interests" who would not yield to new facts.
These are serious accusations and if there is a shred of truth in them, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that there ought to be a thorough investigation of the matter and General Simonds ought to be summoned before that committee to give evidence and to submit himself to serious questioning by the members of this house. It cannot be done, of course, unless we do have a committee.
General Macklin has also made some pretty pointed remarks about our defence policy and he should also be heard. I am not going to weary the committee by quoting what he had to say, but he did declare that Canada's missile radar defence could not possibly stop all the bombers, nor could it warn of guided missiles coming into our country. Well, let us get these men before us and any others who have been free in providing criticism and accusations. Let us get them before that committee and let us examine them most thoroughly and ask them to substantiate the things they have said. It does seem important for us to know. I say we cannot know unless we have some such thing as the committee about which I have spoken.
Let rhe say a word about our position with regard to NORAD. There has been for some

days in this house not a continuous debate but a continuing one about the joint air defence of America. I would just like to say one word about it. It seems clear to me that Canada just would not have the manpower and other resources to defend all of Canadian territory in case of an attack and do it by itself; consequently, in my judgment, we will need the assistance of the United States which does have the manpower and the armed strength. Since this is so, there must be some form of agreement between Canada and the United States regarding the joint defence of North America.
The minister mentioned this morning that this agreement was in the process of development. The procedure and the details are in the process of being worked out. I thought there was nothing peculiar or unusual about that. One hardly expects to enter into an agreement with any other country without first having established the formal and detailed basis upon which an agreement of that kind can be made and be made successfully. For that reason I thought the minister's explanation this morning was quite clear and to me quite sensible. The agreement which is being worked out, however, must make provision for continuation of United States radar and other bases in the northern part of Canada.
We must never allow Canada to become a no man's land between an attacking country and the United States. We insist, therefore, that the defence of Canada must start in the far north. That being the case, we have to join with the United States, it seems to me, in providing the strongest type of warning lines in the north and keep them up to date. I see no alternative to it at the moment unless, Mr. Chairman, it is possible to get such men as General Simonds and those other experts who volunteer information outside the house to come in and give us the information in evidence before the committee and have them undergo careful questioning. If they can show us where it is foolish to spend our money on those northern radar lines then, of course, it would be possible for us to make the necessary change.
We believe that any joint continental air command must be in a position to move to the defence of our country instantly when the attacker has been spotted. There will be no time for consultation once the attack has been launched. We believe that the form of the agreement should provide for whatever Canadian units are to be involved and to be used along with United States units to meet any danger that arises without any further consultation about who is to issue the command or under what circumstances the units
Supply-National Defence are to be used. However, we do believe that parliament should be given the general facts about the agreement as quickly as it has been developed and before action is taken to involve any of our units in any action.
I do not mean to say by that that the details of strategy and all that sort of thing should be divulged to parliament. Nor do I even suggest meeting in camera to hear the details. I refer only to the general form of the agreement, together with the facts about what part Canada is expected to play, who is to command the forces and whether Canadian units can be ordered into action without further consultation with the government or parliament. Once this parliament has approved the general agreement with the United States, then I think all haggling over details should stop.
I should like to say before my time lapses, Mr. Chairman, that I realize some of the problems the new Minister of Defence is up against. I know they must be terrific and I have to make allowances in anything that I say for the short time in which he has been Minister of National Defence; but I have also to keep in mind the many years during which he has been a leading military figure in our country. I give him credit for approaching his task with realism and I do hope he will be successful in effecting those savings of which he spoke, and I think he will be. I do not think there is any question about it. But one of the great problems he faces is the decision about weapons that Canada is developing or already has. Whether we should continue on with the use of conventional weapons or whether we should scrap those, stop all the work on the development of further supersonic jet planes, and that sort of thing and try something else, I do not know.
I am sure that the minister himself is struggling with that problem, but as he struggles with it I am quite certain he will come face to face with the urgent need in this country of better trained, more skilful research and scientific personnel. Various papers in the country for several months past have been emphasizing the need to divert some of the millions of dollars now being spent on defence into the better education and better training of engineers, technologists and skilled researchers. This raises in my mind the question of whether Canada's most effective contribution to defence against aggression might not be the spending of some millions of dollars on research and financing the technical training of a great many more Canadians.
I think perhaps that is going to be essential, particularly if what the minister said this morning is to be made a reality, that is,

Supply-National Defence that through the joint efforts of Canada and the United States at the bases in Texas we are to develop interceptors that will be successful in stopping ballistic missiles that are aimed at us and which we can detect in time. I hope the minister will have something to say on that matter before he closes the debate. In fact, in the course of studying his estimates, if we are going to study them right here in committee of supply, it will be my purpose to remind him of the question and perhaps to draw out from him some of his ideas with regard to this important problem.
I agree with him that our participation in NATO, taking our full responsibility therein, is the best way to show our determination to prevent aggression. I do not think there is any question about the need for pooling the strength of the western nations in such an alliance as NATO. I believe what the minister said this morning is perfectly true, that our collective security is bound up in NATO and we must keep ourselves as strong as we possibly can in that connection. We must never let down our guard and the only way we can be sure that other nations will not launch a war against us is by reminding them through some such collective arrangement as NATO that if they do their sins will rebound on their own heads with redoubled force. I feel that alone is one of the best assurances against war so I do not plead for one moment that we should divert needed moneys from the provision of those weapons of war that are essential to prevent aggression. But I do ask the minister to consider most carefully the possibility of diverting some moneys into the proper training and education of the skilled personnel this country is going to need if we are ever going to keep ourselves free from aggressors.
I do not think I will speak longer at this time. There are many questions we would like to ask regarding the details of the estimates and we will do so when they are before the committee. But I ask the minister and the government once more to consider setting up a committee to study the defence estimates before whom we can call experts to give evidence and to justify the things they have so freely said to the newspapers and in addressing clubs and other organizations across this country.
There is only one final thing I wish to say. While we are concentrating our attention on military affairs, on national defence, I think we should also try to keep ourselves balanced. Let us never forget that the moral influence Canada can exert in this troubled world can be much more effective, if it is properly mobilized and exerted, than all the


military weapons that might be piled up put together. We have a place that we can fill and I certainly suggest that we keep our minds on that phase of world affairs as well.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON POLICY RESPECTING SATELLITE STATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the debate on defence is one of the most important debates that comes before parliament. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speeches made thus far. Particularly I should like to make reference briefly to the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I should like very much to agree with everything he said, and there is much with which I can agree, but I cannot agree with any letting down of our guard as far as the security of the country and its people is concerned. Peace does not rest with us. Russia can have peace tomorrow on most favourable terms if she desires it and she can also have war. Whether we have peace or war in this world depends largely on Russia.
It may be news to members of the house that during the 1940's a special committee was set up by the authorities in Russia to study the question of whether they could have co-existence with the western nations or, in other words, whether communism and the free world could live side by side in peace or whether there would have to be war. That committee was composed of some of the most eminent men in Russia at that time. They spent about two years studying the question and brought in their report to the politburo or the supreme praesidium as they call it today.
After studying the question from every angle they came to the conclusion that war between the communist world and the free world was inevitable. You may not subscribe to that and I may not subscribe to that, but that was the essence of their report. It was considered by the ruling body in Russia and was accepted. Furthermore, they set three dates when war would be possible, 1952, 1954 and 1956, but they made the provision that circumstances might arise in the course of the timetable they had set which might extend their recommendations to 1960.
Anybody who has studied and followed Russian methods down through the years can readily see, Mr. Chairman, that right along they have been basing their policy on that report. They have tested the west on more than one occasion. They have tested our preparation to resist in Korea. From Korea they went to southeast Asia and now they are testing us in the Middle East.
On the basis of this information, what are Canada and the free world going to do? It is a well known fact, and it only needs to be stated to be believed because it has been

stated time and time again, that the communists mean world domination and unless we accept peace on their terms we must provide the resistance by which our people may continue to live in a free and democratic way as we are doing today. This raises the question of what we are going to do regarding defence. This is a defence budget. This is a debate on defence, and the whole safety of the nation is bound up in it.
I come from the province of Newfoundland and we have problems there that probably do not apply to the provinces inland. Furthermore, we know what war is at first hand. One only needs to remind this house that we had the submarine menace all around our coast during the last war. From our coast we have seen actual sinkings of ships by German submarines. We have had submarines around our coast since then. A few years ago we had five Russian submarines around our coast. We had reports during the past summer of many submarines-I will not say what they are because I have not that definite information-around our coast. They were reported around our coast continually during the whole summer. I am not so naive as to believe that those submarines were there for friendly purposes.
I raised the question in this house with the Minister of National Defence and let me say that I received from him the greatest cooperation which I appreciate immensely. At his invitation I discussed with him some of the problems which we must face on the east coast, particularly Newfoundland. At his request I wrote to him and gave him my views. He acknowledged that letter in a very nice way and said that he would take the matter up with his department and look into my proposals. I do not propose to quote from my letter to the minister in any way with regard to security but perhaps if I quote some parts of it this house may be given some idea of what is in my mind. I shall quote some parts of the letter which I think I can quote without involving security. In my letter to the minister I said this:
The submarine menace to our shipping in case of hostilities is no figment of the imagination but a reality in view of recent events taking place around the shores of Newfoundland for some time. When it is known that Russia has about 500 submarines, numbers of them of the latest model, the danger to our shipping is apparent.
I should like to point out that Newfoundland is very vulnerable to this danger, chiefly because almost all our needs, including food, is imported by water. If this supply is severed, great hardships will ensue and it will be the first duty of Canada to supply our people of Newfoundland with food, etc., and the only way this can be done will be by air.
Supply-National Defence
I made recommendations which I will not specify because I think they can be classified under security but I ended up in this way:
I shall be happy to further discuss those proposals with you or your officials at any time.
I think that clearly sets out the position in which we shall find ourselves in Newfoundland in case of hostilities. That is not all. In his remarks today-and I shall paraphrase them-the minister gave some assurance to this house that the submarine menace is being taken care of. But shortly afterwards he also said that the submarine menace was receiving the most careful consideration. I agree with the minister in what he said there. I do not want this house to take my word alone with regard to the seriousness of this submarine menace. I shall quote two or three articles and I shall be as brief as I can. This statement is by Field Marshal Viscount Montgomery. It is from Chatham, England. The article states as follows:
Field Marshal Viscount Montgomery, Deputy Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, said that control of the seas still is more important than guided missiles.
I have here a report from Paris which reads as follows:
U.S. Admiral Jerauld Wright warned today that Russia is building a huge navy designed to isolate North America from Europe and destroy the North Atlantic Treaty Organization . . .
The Admiral said that Russia has developed the largest submarine fleet ever known in peacetime.
Moscow is building a navy larger than all the others in the world combined except for the U.S. navy, he said, for the purpose of "the isolation of North America from Europe, the defeat of NATO at sea and therefore the destruction of our alliance".
I think I have said enough to draw the attention of this house to the seriousness of the submarine menace. The latest designed submarine the United States had, powered by atomic energy, left a year or so ago to manoeuvre. I think she left in the vicinity of the Azores. She was to penetrate the defences of North America within certain defined limits in order to test the defences against the modern submarine. She set out on her course and was detected by the anti-submarine detection of one of the United States destroyers. However, she promptly got away from it. She penetrated all their defences, surfaced around Cape Cod and then wirelessed to the authorities what she had done. If she had not been circumscribed and kept within limits-she could not go out of those limits-she could very easily have evaded the destroyers that sighted her by their detection devices. But she was within those limits; and even within those limits she penetrated all the defences we had -that was about a year or so ago-and then she surfaced.

Supply-National Defence
I look upon defence against the submarine menace as vital to the safety of Canada. I look upon it as vital to the safety of the troops overseas and the supplying of our allies. This morning the minister said something with which I agree and I again paraphrase what he said. He stated that we cannot in the first phase of war by sea use our shipping. I agree with that statement. We have Canadian forces overseas. We have allies in Europe, particularly in Great Britain. We are vulnerable to the submarine menace. We in Newfoundland shall need food in a very short time if hostilities break out. From what I can understand, Great Britain today has only about three weeks' to one month's food supply bn hand. If this submarine menace is as dangerous and threatening as I have tried to point out, and as I believe to be absolutely true, then the only way in which we can supply the province of Newfoundland and our allies is by air. That stands to reason. We have not the facilities with which to do it and it is time we woke up to the fact that we should have them.
This is a point about which I am greatly concerned. I think the authorities here, particularly in the higher command, must wake up to this fact also. We have co-ordination in our forces and I am glad to pay tribute to it. I believe we have good co-ordination in the lower ranks. However, I am not too sure that we have it in the higher ranks. When you hear retired generals criticizing what the higher command does, and in no uncertain terms, one is left to wonder what is wrong with our higher command. I am not against differences of opinion between the army, the navy and the air force and even within those services; that is all to the good, but when those services are shown up before the general public as being inadequate and not only the general public but the members of the forces themselves realize this indecision which is taking place in the higher command, how can you expect the morale of our troops to be kept at the pitch which we all desire?
I think it is high time that our higher command got together. I do not care whether they call in General Simonds or General Macklin or whoever they call in, but I think they should get together and iron out these things and tell this country where we stand. This uneasiness with respect to our higher command today is penetrating down to the ranks and it is having an effect on the morale of the troops. From what little knowledge I have, it would seem that some of our troops in the different services are seriously considering giving up their careers and going back into civilian life because they are


afraid they are going to be disbanded and cast out upon a cold and hungry world with no prospects of work.
Now I have one final word to say on this united command. I may take a different attitude from some of my colleagues on this side of the house. As you know, we have in Newfoundland the United States strategic air force and in that province we are dependent principally upon those forces for our defence. Let that be understood, there is no mistake about it. Now I asked the minister who would give the orders to this strategic air force in Newfoundland in the case of an emergency when it would have to go into action and the minister very courteously informed me that this strategic force would get its orders from St. Hubert. Well I have nothing against that, but I understand the headquarters of the strategic air force is in Colorado Springs. Then we have another command in St. Hubert and we have this air force operating in Newfoundland and I think also in Labrador, certainly in Greenland.
Now my suggestion to the minister, which I put in all sincerity, is that he should, without any waste of time, look into this business and get it ironed out so that everybody will know exactly where they stand. If General Partridge has the authority to order action on the part of the United States forces or the Canadian forces-I do not care whether it is on Canadian or United States territory then he should not have any strings attached to that authority in the case of necessity. He should have full authority to issue orders immediately without having to wait to contact Ottawa, or contact the minister or the Prime Minister and then have them contact St. Hubert and St. Hubert contact the forces in Newfoundland. We are getting into a state now where I think war is liable to take place and if you give authority-I do not care whether it is to an United States general or a Canadian marshal as long as you think the man is fitted for his position-then I think the time has come for instructions to be given to him in such a way that there will be no waste of time but that he should have full power to order troops into action without having one hand tied behind his back. He should be in a position to act immediately if an emergency arises. I do not care whether the forces fly over our territory or over United States territory so long as they do a good job in defending the people of the North American continent.
I think what the minister has done is to settle political questions before setting up the co-ordination of his military responsibilities. May I say in all sincerity that I

think he has put the cart before the horse- whether it was done by the former government or his government is immaterial to me but he has now settled political questions before military ones which I think is wrong and the first step should be the setting up of the military command. I ask the minister, for the safety of the people of the North American continent, to get this question settled and settled quickly so that there will be no trouble in the event of hostilities and there will be no waste of time.
I have one further suggestion to make and that is with regard to food supplies in Great Britain. Our western friends may appreciate this point. If Great Britain is to be an ally and to play her full part in NATO she cannot do so unless she has food. Now I make this suggestion for what it is worth: I think we should help Great Britain by putting food supplies in that country, and I include grain and other things, which would last between four and six months and which could be stored in case of emergency.

speechtext: Furthermore, I suggest that Great Britain should use those supplies as she needs them day by day and they can be replenished as necessary. I say this because I am convinced if these hostilities should arise, then automatically it becomes obvious that we shall have to supply Great Britain with food and the only way to do so would be by air. Mr. Chairman, I do not think there are too many points which could be added to those raised by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in his excellent speech this afternoon. I do believe however that his point of view should be buttressed as much as possible in order that it may be given full consideration by the government, because I think there is a definite need which is becoming more apparent by the day for a review of the role filled by our Department of National Defence. I think we have to get away from the Maginot line philosophy which was enunciated by the hon. member for Trinity-Conception where We think in terms of a 1914-1918 war or a 1940-45 war. We now have to gear ourselves
Supply-National Defence to developments which have taken place within the last month and a half and consider the effects which those developments have upon our defence.
When the Minister of National Defence was first appointed to his post I fully expected he might follow the pattern set down by Great Britain in the announcement that there would be reductions in the defence expenditures. At that time, I think, a lot of consideration had in fact been given to this point. However, shortly after he took office an announcement was made that a lot of his criticism had been unfounded and that there would be no significant changes in the defence expenditures. I think at this time, as pointed out by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, it is virtually impossible to make any significant changes in the estimates because the greater part of the year has passed by and it would be most difficult to make reductions in expenditures which would be meaningful.
I believe the comment of the minister, when he was asked to remark on the launching of the Russian sputnik, was that it was "out of this world". I think that comment was something from which we should take our keynote and start gearing our defence thinking to procedures which might, at the moment, seem to be out of this world, but which will be upon us in the very near future.
We already see newspaper speculation about the date of the launching of a rocket to the moon. There is an indication that in five or seven years they may be able to construct manned satellites capable of going to Mars and returning. This seems as spectacular to us now as the invention of gunpowder might have seemed to someone in prehistoric times. We must be aware of the tremendous developments which are taking place in the applications of science to the techniques of destruction, and I think we should ask ourselves just where Canada stands in this great arms race between Russia and the United States. It seems to me that we are in the position of a kindergarten pupil running in the senior foot race. Yes, we get there, but we are so far behind that we might just as well not be in the running. I mean by that, of course, that with our limited resources we can never hope to compete against the scientific development which goes on in the United States and in Russia.
I think an example of this could be cited in the Arrow, the CF-105, which, I believe, cost us over $200 million and perhaps as much as $300 million to design. It has been admitted that this plane is virtually obsolescent before deliveries have been made. We cannot possibly derive much pleasure from the thought of spending $200 or $300 million

Supply-National Defence upon an aircraft which is obsolete. I recognize immediately that in the course of experimental research expenditures are necessary, and that all the expenditures do not pay dividends. But I think we must consider the effectiveness of this expenditure, because Canada over a number of years has spent billions of dollars-the present estimates cover an expenditure of $1,700 million -and can anyone here honestly say that through the expenditure of all this money we now have a defence. We are all aware of the fact that we depend on the strategic air command of the United States for our defence and for the power of retaliation in the event of attack. We are dependent also on the forces of NATO to provide the unified defensive force of the western world.
Having in mind the startling scientific developments which have taken place abroad, and thinking of the jet bombers now being flown by the strategic air command, we can very easily ask ourselves just what is the role of manpower, or what is the limitation of human beings in future air warfare. Air Marshal Joubert of Great Britain recently wrote a book on rockets in which he dealt extensively with the developments which have taken place in Germany, in Peenemiinde, beginning as far back as 1934. He gave evidence to show that had Hitler been as impressed by the technique of rocketry as he was by more conventional aircraft there might have been a tragic difference in the outcome of the second world war.
Air Marshal Joubert asks: what is the limitation on a human being? We find that in aircraft travelling at many hundreds of miles an hour, one, or even two pilots cannot cope with the machine because of the tremendous speed reached and the comparatively slow reaction time of a human being. We are wondering just what is the role of the piloted aircraft in the face of the development which will be taking place in the next three or four years.
Over the past number of years we have prided ourselves, or at least some hon. members have done so, over the radar defence lines, the mid-Canada line, the "Pinetree" line and the distant early warning line. We may very well ask ourselves now how effective these devices will be in face of the intercontinental ballistic missile or the intermediate ballistic missiles. I believe the present radar installations are limited to a range of 70,000 feet. How effective are they going to be in detecting a missile travelling at an altitude of three or four hundred miles?
I have a feeling that our defence budgets over the years have been drawn up by the generals, the field marshals and the admirals.


I think it is very understandable that as they go through the echelons of these various services they should make efforts to maintain establishments. As the budget is drawn up, a certain colonel is going to try to maintain his establishment; he does not like to see his position made unnecessary. I think there is an undue amount of pressure applied for the sake of maintaining establishments which no longer perform their role in the defence of this country.
I should like to endorse to the best of my ability the suggestion which was made by my leader, and which has been made repeatedly in this house by members and supporters of the government when in opposition and by present members of the opposition, namely that we should establish a defence estimates committee to enquire into all aspects of the expenditure of these huge sums of money. I think this is most necessary, and that any consideration of defence expenditures should bear in mind not only military aspects of the matter, but that economic and political considerations should be brought to the forefront.
Speaking as a layman on military matters, and that is in fact what most of us are- I am one who did most of my military work as a foot slogger-it appears to me that one development which can be made toward the modernization of our armed forces would be to unify our armed services. I can see that in former wars there was need for an army, a navy and an air force because each was performing a specialized role. But today, with the development of the hydrogen bomb and nuclear weapons, I think consideration could be given by the government to the unification of all our armed services under one command, whether it is to be called the defence force, the armed service force or anything else. I think economies could be made administratively by this means, and I think, also, that a decision such as this would assist in establishing the chain of command.
One obvious argument in favour of this suggestion is the present situation in the United States where there is great rivalry between the navy and the army as to which service is going to launch the first successful rocket. This has led to the ridiculous situation where two branches of the armed services of a country are competing against each other instead of pooling their knowledge, and I have a suspicion that we Canadians are not completely immune from the criticism which must be directed against such folly.
It would seem to me that with the developments which have taken place in the last few years the question of manpower has become

relatively unimportant. It is true that in terms of small localized wars men are necessary, but manpower will not win wars against nuclear weapons. The suggestion which has been made by this group is that a United Nations police force be established to provide sufficient manpower to control any localized outburst or any small wars.
We must look upon nuclear weapons as provoking all-out war or none at all in view of these technological advances. I think, too, that in future estimates a second look should be given to the role of the militia in Canada. I notice that announcements have been made indicating changes which are being proposed in the role of the militia. We might as well face the fact that they can throw away all the old British 303 Enfields and Sten guns because they will never have the opportunity of using them.
When I visited NATO headquarters in 1954 I had the pleasure of hearing Field Marshal Lord Montgomery address us and he pointed out at that time the hopelessness of getting a militia trained in time to go into action in a modern war. It would require at the least three months to get a militia man trained so he could take part in modern combat. I think most of us are of the impression that if a nuclear war is launched we will not have three months for preparations of this kind.
The militia might very well be geared to playing a most useful role connected with civil defence. They should be provided with radiation indicators so they would be able to determine if in fact radiation were present to a harmful degree. They should be trained to fight fires and to deal with similar local emergencies. If this were done they would be fulfilling a useful role and I am certain that those who are members of the militia would be happier to know that they in fact had a more vital part to play in the defence of Canada than is the case at the present time.
It would seem also that a suggestion could be made related to the example of NATO. In NATO we as nations have each given up a bit of our sovereignty for our common defence and I think Canada's role in defence could be given further consideration in the light of this fact. We cannot ever hope to compete against the United States and Russia in the arms race but it would appear to me that if some agreement could be arrived at where we as a country were to specialize in some particular phase of defence we would be making an even greater contribution to the common defence of the western world. If we were to concentrate on the various aspects of rockets and if the major portion of our defence role were to be geared to scientific development perhaps in the long run we would achieve
Supply-National Defence further protection. I believe we must be careful, however, in any such arrangement to safeguard some aspects of our sovereignty in that no foreign power should be allowed to involve us in a war without our consent. That is the point at issue in discussions of NORAD at the present time, the concern that the United States might possibly control certain Canadian forces.
I want to emphasize again the request that future estimates of the Department of National Defence should be reduced to give consideration to the new look which we are presently taking in external affairs and which we should also be taking in terms of our defence expenditures. Recent scientific developments have produced a tremendous change and we should not be trapped into a Maginot line philosophy. We must put ourselves in a position to progress with the times. This will require a re-allocation of defence expenditures a larger portion of which of necessity must be channelized through our universities in the form of scientific research which along with giving us military defence will assist in the progress of our country and of humanity in general.
The second prong of this approach, as it were, must be to give further consideration to abolishing the causes of war. As we look back through history we find that war in the main has been caused by greed, hunger and oppression. As long as we can look around the world today and see countries which are in a relatively backward state who look with envy at the advanced standard of living that prevails in western countries we are leaving the door open to a furthering of the causes of communism. Discontent will exist in those countries and the forces of communism will be received only too readily. It is the challenge of the western nations to fulfil their responsibilities to these countries of the world which are sometimes referred to as backward-but which are more accurately described as underprivileged-which have been dominated by other countries over the centuries and now have a lower standard of living than ours. We must give consideration to applying some of our defence budget to the supplying of food to these countries through our national organizations and the United Nations so the prevailing standards of living can be raised in these countries and they may become real allies of free humanity.

Mr. Chairman, other speakers have covered in a general way much of the ground I intend to cover and I agree with most of what has been said. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in his remarks brought out some excellent points worthy of the careful and earnest consideration of this

Supply-National Defence committee but I would say to him and to all hon. members that we must lace the difficult international situation with our eyes open. Idealism will not counter communism and the outstretched hand must be backed by strength when it is offered to one who lor years has shown no disposition to accept a hand that is offered in peace and good will.
I listened with a great deal ol interest to the outline ol our position as given by the minister this morning. I will give his statement very close reading tomorrow and I am sure we all will have a much broader knowledge and understanding ol the condition in which we find ourselves at the present time. I did observe that he referred at length to the part we play in the Far East, the Near East, the Middle East and NATO. We are glad to know that our nation is taking its rightful place in defence ol the western nations. These are important considerations from an international point of view to prevent aggression and to demonstrate our preparedness to retaliate effectively and promptly in case of attack but I believe our people are more intimately concerned with the possible direct attack on the North American continent and will not be satisfied until they know that no effort is being spared to guarantee the greatest possible degree of defence in the face of modern methods of direct attack. Future attacks, we believe, will come from long-range missiles, long-range bombers and long-range submarines and these may be based miles beyond our borders.
In the face of that, Mr. Chairman, our people want some assurances that very careful attention is being given to this possibility by our defence department and that science is being mobilized to the full to study and to try to find an answer to this very serious problem.
Now, in regard to the estimates proper, it is hard to get down to details when we find that an immense amount of $1,670,000,000 is lumped in one item. It is impossible, as I said, to give any detailed consideration to those estimates and therefore we must deal with them in a very general way. However, when we are considering the expenditure of such a large sum of money

and the taxpayer's money-we who are the representatives of the taxpayers in this house have the responsibility of seeing that this expenditure is given careful consideration. To do that job intelligently, Mr. Chairman, we must have information.
It is certainly discouraging when we find ourselves in the position in which the Minister of National Defence found himself some months ago when he assumed the important office which he now holds. Shortly after
IMr. McLeod.]
assuming office, according to the press, he is reported to have made a statement along these lines: "My criticism of the Department of National Defence in the past was based upon lack of information". This is another way of saying that it was based on ignorance of what was going on. I am not using the word "ignorance" with any personal implications; but I am emphasizing this point to show that we members of this house must be kept informed, and it is to the government of the day that we look for this information. But, Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to say that under this present administration, although we were promised greater personal responsibility as members and greater responsibility as a parliament, we find that we are kept in the same state of ignorance as we were when the Liberals were in power. According to the old saying, ignorance is bliss; but in matters that affect our international relationships and our national well-being and our people's pocketbooks so much as does this national defence spending and national defence policies, we should not be kept in ignorance.
The people of Canada do not object to heavy defence spending, provided they are satisfied the department is looking after their defence efficiently and is giving value for the money spent. In order to keep our people satisfied there must be a feeling of confidence in the administration which can only be fostered by giving out a reasonable amount of information of what is being done. We do not expect that many of the secret arrangements which are being planned among the various top officials of the different organizations to preserve and to defend our western nations should be given to us. We are not looking for that kind of information; but I would say to the minister that we as members of parliament have, I think, passed the age when we may have been looked upon as juveniles. I do believe that we are responsible and are able to decide in our own minds that which can be given, that which can be publicized and that which cannot.
In order to see that that information is given to us I would certainly support the recommendations that have been made by every speaker thus far for a committee on national defence. That committee, Mr. Chairman, should be a permanent committee; it should not be too large. Besides studying the policies and the expenditures of the department, it could also act in an advisory capacity to the minister of the department which means so much to us and to our future welfare. Our party made the same request in discussing our external affairs problems and we think that in those two fields, so closely

linked, the parliament of Canada should stand united. To do so, though, parliament must have some say in formulating policy and in carrying out that policy. 1 mentioned the two fields of defence and external affairs as being closely linked. I would go farther, Mr. Chairman, and say that they are interlocking. For that reason certain aspects of our integrated defence policy with the United States give us cause for alarm. We, as a proud and aggressive people, are jealous of our sovereign rights. We have bravely and boldly stood for those rights since confederation and I hope it will always be our guiding principle in dealing with other nations.
Expressions have been made by responsible officials of a foreign, though quite friendly nation, that under integration we shall have lost some of those rights. I am glad to note that our Minister of National Defence and our Prime Minister have repudiated those statements; yet I am sure that in the minds of all of us we cannot conceive of such a responsible member of another government making such statements unless there was basis in fact for those remarks.
I am going to say with all the force at my command that we are in favour of integration. We believe it is one way to make the best use of our defensive power, but we say that it must be a temporary arrangement and one which is not irrevocable. Then, since it is so closely linked with our external affairs, the whole plan should have been worked out in conjunction and consultation with the Department of External Affairs.
Instead, what do we find? We find the same ignorance on the part of the Department of External Affairs that I say we as members of this house are faced with when we are giving consideration to the estimates of the department. I am going to refer to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of December 4 in its report of the session of the committee on external affairs. I am going to read just briefly. It appears that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was being interrogated about the progress that had been made and negotiations, if any, that had been carried on. He is reported as having said that his department was not concerned.
The word "concerned" there is in quotation marks. I cannot countenance that the Secretary of State for External Affairs of this country would say that his department was not concerned in such a state of affairs. I am sure there must be something wrong despite the fact that the word "concerned" is in quotation marks. In any event, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that his department was not concerned in the arrangements that had led to the establishment of the command. If that is a fact, 96698-122

We have also heard that negotiations are taking place at the service level and with respect to that the minister replied that negotiations were being conducted at the service level and that the two commanders are now working out recommendations on the basis of which there will be an intergovernmental exchange of notes specifying the command's terms of reference. One member who just spoke said that the cart had been placed before the horse and I think he used a very apt expression to describe these negotiations.
To me, Mr. Chairman, this is a most serious reflection on the Department of External Affairs when we see something that will affect the political well-being of Canada for years to come being handled by the military authorities. In fact, it would appear that the service commanders are now drawing up political terms which when completed will be turned over to the two governments. That is something which must not go unchallenged. In fact, it is a challenge to the civil authority which must always remain supreme. The Department of National Defence, responsible to the government of Canada and through it to the people of Canada, must take no action to override the civil authority.
We can look back through the history of Britain and the history of Canada since confederation and see that the civil authority has always been supreme. Now we have a serious threat that our military officials are going to dictate to the civil authority of Canada plans and policies which will become effective and which will govern us to some degree for many years to come.

However, in so doing I do not intend to set myself up as a military expert in any way or even a critic of national defence. I am sure the minister can almost foretell what I am about to mention as he has been spoken to in this regard before. I hope he does not feel I work under the principle that the squeaking wheel gets the grease, although I will admit it has certain merits in certain places.

I want to ask the minister and the department to give serious reconsideration to the matter of certain moneys which were in the estimates brought down by the former minister of national defence last spring. Certain moneys were set aside for the building of very necessary accommodation in Sudbury.
I am sure the minister had a first-hand opportunity to see the trying conditions under which the military people in our area are working when he paid us a visit on November 10 and graciously assisted in the unveiling of a new cenotaph.
There is a unique situation in the city of Sudbury regarding the proposed building and I should like to bring it to the attention of the house. I think hon. members will all agree that as soon as a suggestion is heard in a community that the government intends to buy some property for the erection of any kind of building the land automatically goes up in price, possibly to a great many times its real value. Such is not the case in our city. A few years ago a public-spirited citizen donated a parcel of land amounting to approximately 5.6 acres for which he paid $10,000. The land is now being held by the crown and the stipulation was made that an armoury would be built thereon. The land was received in the Queen's name by the previous minister of national defence, and in his estimates of last spring he attempted to fulfil his promise to make the building a reality.
I understand that the Department of Public Works feels it is being overcharged most outrageously for the properties now being occupied in view of the accommodation that is supplied. A year ago I was asked to intervene in the matter to see if the owners of the buildings would reduce the rent. I may say I was successful in having it reduced somewhat but I also feel that the rent is still exorbitant. Of course, the owners of the buildings take the view that they are not particularly anxious to rent them for the purpose for which they are now being used and as far as they are concerned they feel they would receive a greater monetary return from new buildings which they would be pleased to construct.
Unfortunately, the property now being held by the crown is affected by a proviso in the agreement of sale between the former owner of the property and the gentleman who donated it to the crown and that proviso is that if an armoury should not be built on this location the land will revert to the original owner at the original price. This land has been examined and tested by the engineers of the department. I am not prepared to prove this but I understand that plans were drawn up for the erection of the building but they are now pigeonholed.

The reason I am on my feet today is to make a serious appeal to the minister and the department to reconsider their decision not to erect this building at the present time.
I feel that we will lose the property which was given to us for this purpose if action is not taken soon and I also believe that we are paying an exorbitant rent for the premises now occupied. I am deadly serious about this request to the department and I hope the minister will see fit to reconsider the matter very shortly.

Mr. Chairman, I have a brief word. I appreciated very much the Minister of National Defence allowing us a few days ago to hear one of our distinguished generals. By the outlines on the charts, and we can see those outlines yet, he showed us what Canada was doing and what it was prepared to do. The reason I rose at this time is to say that it is not aeroplanes that win the war. Neither is it submarines or bombs. I ask what it was that defeated Germany in the last war. They had the best equipped army in the world. They had more aeroplanes and more submarines than any other country. They had everything that would indicate that Germany was going to win. Why did Germany not win? If they had had more aeroplanes, would they have won?
A call went out across the country, Mr. Chairman, for a day of prayer. That was a big day not only here but in other countries. What happened? Germany made three outstanding mistakes. The Germans were clever. Germany was supposed to have the best brains in the world. Our students used to go there in order to complete their education, as they thought; but they did not do so. What were the three mistakes? After Dunkirk, when the allies were beaten, the first mistake they made was that they did not wipe England off the map. Why did they not do so? That was the first mistake they made. The next mistake was Pearl Harbor. Why was the attack made on Pearl Harbor? The attack was made because they thought it would help win the war. But what did it do? It brought the United States wholeheartedly into the war. The third mistake they made was that they attacked Russia and kept on attacking her with the result that they were finally beaten. I can hear so many in the opposition saying "Too little and too late"; but you are never too late when God is first and when your men rally behind you in the way our Canadian youth did. That is why we won the war.

speechtext:
In following the fine rousing remarks of the hon. member for Fort William and the equally fine remarks of the hon. member for Trinity-Conception as opposed to the spirit of fatalism and of defeat breathed

by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, it seems to me that it is fitting that just a few more things be said. If we say that we simply cannot win and if we give up, we do not give the Lord a chance to play a part at all. We may not be able to do very much when we start, as was the case in the battle of Britain in world war II, but if we do all that we possibly can and if we rely on the God of battles, we shall have a chance of winning. My feeling is that it is very much the same as we approach this dreadful crisis in world history, the worst the world has ever known.
It seems to me also that we should give a little bit of thought to another matter which was referred to indirectly by the hon. member for Trinity-Conception. I refer to the kind of people we are opposed to. Most people think it is the Russian people we are opposed to. That is the last thing in the world we are opposed to. We are opposed to the group of men who conquered Russia in the so-called revolution back in 1917, who now rule Russia with an iron hand and who intend to extend that sordid rule over all the people of the world. There is no use in talking about coexistence with those people. With them it is all or none. They talk co-existence but it is the last thing they think of.
May I refer to the remarks of three of their leaders. I mention Lenin first. In 1923 Lenin announced to the world-or so it would be announced to the world-that it would be unnecessary to defeat the United States in a military way, that she would fall into their hands like an over-ripe fruit. All that is necessary is that enough people in Canada and the United States speak as did the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and the whole of North America will fall into their hands like an overripe fruit.
The next communist leader who said a most significant thing in this respect was Manuilsky. This man, if I recall it correctly, spoke in 1930. He said this-these are not his exact words; I am not quoting; I am speaking from memory-"We will put on a peace offensive which will surpass anything the world ever saw and when we get them all softened up we will smash them with the iron fist". If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had wanted to play right into Manuilsky's hands or into Lenin's, he could not have done it better.
The next man is Khrushchev. I cannot remember just exactly what it was that Khrushchev said, but fairly recently he made a remark which I have already put on the record in times past and which did not in any way indicate that he had receded from the position of Lenin and Manuilsky but rather that he was following on as a member in the team, aiming to accomplish the thing which 96698-1224

May I repeat once more that we are not fighting the Russians; we are not fighting the Chinese; we are not fighting any of the people who have come under the domination of the so-called communist organization which is another outfit entirely, parading under the mask of communism. We are not fighting the peoples who are their fronts; we are fighting the men hidden behind communism. Let us never forget that fact.
While we are on the subject may I suggest to the Minister of National Defence that, with all the ardour of his being, he impress upon the leaders of the United States, Great Britain and the other NATO nations that if they do not single out those men in their governments who are agents of that group of people who are behind communism it will do no good at all to find out new secrets, because those secrets will be in the hands of Moscow before we ourselves hear about them.
I have taken occasion to refer to this matter two or three times in the house previously. Some people have supposed that there is nothing to what I have said. May I say that it will be a great deal better if they can learn now than at some later time when they will say, "Oh, if I had only known". It could have been known but they were just simply too narrow-minded and blind to listen, so that they could have been told.
May I urge upon the minister that he take the utmost care with regard to this matter. Let me remind him that immediately after the first satellite went up from Russia, Gouzenko who is in a position to know a great deal more about the matter than does anybody in this house or probably anyone else in this country, announced to the people of Canada and the United States, as far as he could cause his voice to be heard, that the Russians had put the first satellite into the air because the secrets which the United States and Canada had discovered had been transmitted to Russia by people imbedded in the administrations of our countries.
