speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am aware
that the estimates now before the house were prepared by the former administration and, as a supporter of that administration and of that party, I naturally support these estimates. We have before us expenditures of over $1.7 billion for various kinds of military offensive and defensive weapons. We all regret that so much money has to be diverted into unproductive channels when it could be used in so many other ways for human betterment but we realize that this expenditure for military weapons is necessary even if some of the equipment becomes obsolete before it becomes operational.
It is right and fitting that we should make every possible preparation for possible war- a war which we hope will never come-but it does cause me some concern, as it has caused me concern every year since I have been here that we should make an effort to provide for war which does not exist at the present time and yet seem to be so unconcerned about a war which does exist at the present time, a war which in fact has been going on continuously for the last 40 years and which has recently entered a new and decisive phase. I refer, of course, to the war of ideas.
We have become almost panic-stricken because soviet Russia has taken away our lead by launching sputniks and guided missiles. Yet, on the other hand, we are extremely apathetic, complacent and indifferent about an even more deadly weapon, the communist ideology, to which I understand my hon. friend from Lethbridge was referring a few moments ago. Military weapons are not the only means of fighting a war or of protecting ourselves against war, there are political weapons and economic weapons. In soviet Russia, however, military, economic and political weapons are all controlled by and subordinated to their ideology. Our hysteria about the sputniks and the ICBM's is exactly what Russia wants at this time because it diverts our attention from their ideological weapons upon which they are relying for
[Mr. Blackmore.I

ultimate victory and it diverts also our attention from the necessity of developing ideological counter weapons of our own.
The word ideology is one which we use with a certain amount of discomfort. We do not seem to have any very clear idea of what it means. We use it in a casual and offhand manner, but we do not take the trouble to analyse or to dissect it and we are very often content to confuse it with idealism, as did my hon. friend from Macleod when he spoke earlier in this debate. An ideology is an idea in action; an idea that includes a plan for remaking the world; an idea that has become a force because it has captured the hearts and souls of human beings to such an extent that they are prepared to give everything they have to assure its triumph. Over the years the anti-democratic countries have perfected ideological weapons, techniques and strategies; they have won many countries with the force of their ideas alone and without firing a single shot. We try to counteract that purely by military political and economic means.
By means of their ideology the communists can achieve and have achieved the following objectives and during the period of coexistence it is upon the achievement of these objectives that they rely for ultimate victory. Now the first objective they seek to attain is to destroy and weaken our belief in the central values which the democratic nations wish to preserve and endeavour to defend. What are we doing to counteract that? What are we doing to build up our defences against it? The second objective is to undermine confidence in the ability and the moral integrity of national leadership, that is, of all politicians, military and administrative leaders and those with whom the citizens are in contact and who have their confidence. The third objective is to weaken the ability and the willingness of a nation to co-operate for common aims by destroying group solidarity. In the fourth place they seek to destroy the peoples' psychic equilibrium and personal adjustment to existing conditions.
These objectives are being achieved by the communist ideology right here in Canada, and that is something about which we cannot feel too complacent. As the hon. member for Lethbridge pointed out, it is not necessary for everyone in a nation to be a committed communist; Lenin took over Russia with only 11,000 of them, a hard core of 11,000 people committed to his ideology. I am told by a reliable source that there are about 8,000 committed communists in Canada at the present time. When we consider the defence of our country we must consider all aspects of defence, not the military aspect only.

The minister pointed out that our policy is based on collective security within the framework of NATO. That collective security is only as strong as NATO's ability and will to resist and to act decisively; it is only as strong as NATO's unity. And what is NATO's unity based on today? It is based on fear, and it is hardly strong enough to withstand the internal stresses and strains of conflicting self interest among member nations. What NATO needs primarily, and what we need, I think, to contribute to NATO is a positive and moral ideology which is capable of counteracting these objectives which I listed a few moments earlier, and capable not only of resisting them but of taking the offensive against them.
The original idea of NATO as a temporary shield while defences were mobilized was sound, but the present idea of NATO as a permanent Maginot line is unsound and that is what NATO has developed into, a ring, as we have been told, of 250 bases. The only difference is that we have armed this modern Maginot line with nuclear weapons and guided missiles instead of the conventional weapons of the old Maginot line. But the fundamental idea is the same, and it is unsound.
In the ideological war, as in the war of arms, the best defence is attack, and in the war of ideas NATO must therefore take the offensive. Earlier today hon. members have spoken about removing the causes of war. I think the hon. member for Kindersley referred to poverty and hunger as among the factors which caused war, and he spoke of them, in the way most of us do, as though they were something separate and apart from ourselves, something abstract, which does not concern us as individuals. That is not so, and I think that is where we have been missing the boat all along. The mess we are in today in external affairs, in the United Nations, in the Middle East and in all the theatres of the world has been brought about by people who have been regarded as being extremely practical. One of the reasons why we have not come to grips with these problems is because we have lacked a positive ideology, and we have lacked a positive ideology because we have thought of these things in the abstract without relating them to ourselves. To develop an ideology we should begin, of course, with ourselves, because as I am so is my nation.
When we, the people of the democratic countries, begin to live out in our lives the things we talk about, then democracy will
Supply-National Defence have an ideology capable of taking the offensive against communism. It would be a good thing, if, as some hon. members have suggested, we could do something about alleviating the hunger in the world. We all sympathize with the hungry nations in Asia; and here we are in Canada with a huge pile of surplus wheat and other food products. It has been suggested that instead of spending money on arms we should use that money to purchase commodities to give to the hungry millions of the world. This, in itself, would be a good thing, but it would not be an ideological move, and it would not serve any ideological purpose because of the very fact that we have a surplus and there is an element of self interest in getting rid of it.
In other words, the situation would be as it was pointed out in an article in the last issue of Maclean's Magazine in which the writer described Canadians as we appear to the have not nations of Asia and Africa. They note that when we give, we give selfishly of our abundance and without any sacrifice. It is the total commitment to an idea which constitutes an ideology and which makes it so effective. The thing which attracts people to communism-wealthy people, learned people, scientific people-is not the communist idea itself so much as the commitment of the people to it, that is, the total commitment of the communists with whom they come into contact.
NATO needs an ideology. Some time ago when the bureau of current affairs was set up I thought that might be the beginning of the development of the ideological training of the armed forces. I noted today that the minister said this bureau was going to be discontinued. I am not criticizing the minister for this, because I do not think the bureau of current affairs has ever served the purpose I hoped it would. I have followed its course over the years. It has probably done some good, but nothing which was vital to the needs of the day. I agree with the minister that there are things more pressing and more urgent. But I cannot agree that there is anything more urgent today than the development of ideological training for our services and for our people, and I think the armed services would provide a good starting point.
I was interested in looking over a Soviet news bulletin some time ago in which an explanation was given of the demotion of Marshal Zhukov. I am not going to read all the relevant parts, but I can paraphrase what the bulletin said. What it amounted to was that Marshal Zhukov was becoming less

Supply-National Defence and less enthusiastic about ideological training in the armed forces. One sentence of the bulletin reads:
Comrade Zhukov by his incorrect actions reduced party organizations to the status of purely educational organs.
Then it went on to say that the other thing that was wrong with Marshal Zhukov was that he was not personally living up to his ideology but was glorifying himself instead of the party principles which made him what he was. As I said before, I would like to see some concern and some recognition of this need on the part of the Conservative government.

While I am on my feet perhaps I might clear up one or two of the points that have been raised. I believe we all agree with the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar that the essential need is to remove, if possible, the causes of war but until there is a realistic disarmament policy I feel we must maintain a reasonable degree of security so that our people can live and carry out their ordinary peaceful avocations.
The hon. member for Fort William, the hon. member for Lethbridge, and the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo have spoken about the ideological aspects of training. It would perhaps be interesting to note that in all units there is carried out a service which to a large extent replaces the work which was being done by the bureau of current affairs and of course the unit officers instruct their men on the day to day events of the world.
The hon. member for Kingston and others seemed to be under the impression that there was some lack of liaison between the Department of External Affairs and the Department of National Defence regarding the arrangements connected with the integrated command of the air defences. The original arrangement started as far back as May 14, 1956 when there was a meeting of the Canadian chiefs of staff and the United States joint chiefs of staff and a decision was made to refer the matter to a joint study group. At

that meeting and all subsequent meetings representatives of the Department of External Affairs were present and that department was conversant with all that was going on. In addition to that, of course, the matter was referred to the cabinet as a whole and, as the Prime Minister stated, it was a government decision to adopt this integrated command.
I wish to assure the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke that I fully appreciate the importance of civil control of the armed forces and under no circumstances will the military be permitted in any way to usurp, or override as he said, the civil authority or dictate to the government of the country. I can assure the hon. member that nothing of that nature is occurring at the present time.
The hon. member for Kingston asked about the question of manpower. Recruiting for all three services has been very good recently and we have the total number of men required to meet our commitments. Of course, there is always a shortage of technical personnel and, as the hon. member for Peace River stated, it is desirable that we give all the encouragement possible to the young men of this country to develop technical and engineering skills. It is for that purpose that research and development grants are made through the defence research board through universities for the encouragement of special projects. Regarding the total of money which is being spent on research at the present time, the estimates show that the sum of $64,796,000 is being spent on research and development. It is rather difficult sometimes, as hon. members will appreciate, to separate research from development but if necessary I could give further information regarding that subject.
The question arose as to whether or not our weapons are obsolete. It is easy to suggest that the weapons of today cannot meet the weapons an enemy may have in the near future. I believe that the weapons we have today are capable of meeting the weapons that any potential enemy has today. I believe our interceptors can intercept any Russian bomber that the Russian air force have today.
We are going one step farther: we are developing this CF-105, which is a supersonic interceptor. It will probably be five years before that CF-105 will be in squadron operation, if it turns out to be entirely satisfactory in every respect. I believe that the CF-105 will then be able to deal with any bomber that the Russians will have five years hence. Of course, it will not be able to deal with the intercontinental missile.
Supply-National Defence
As I tried to point out in the remarks I made this morning, we are members of a team and we take on those tasks and produce those weapons which we consider we are most adapted to provide and whose procurement is within our means. In this partnership team we are providing the manned interceptor to meet the manned bomber. We have not gone into the missile field. The anti-intercontinental ballistic missile will be developed and provided by other partners of our alliance. We hope that there will be an opportunity for us to contribute toward that development, but our particular role in this partnership for the defence of the North American continent is to provide a proportion of the manned interceptors to meet the manned bombers and the best advice that I have, founded on the judgment given by our own military advisers and military advisers from our NATO partners, is that for many years to come there will be manned bombers. In fact, we know, contrary to statements which have been made elsewhere, that the Russians are still developing and producing manned bombers. It may well be, as I stated this morning, that if our deterrent fails and an attack does occur, that attack will be a combination of intercontinental missiles and manned bombers.
It is our sincere hope that the means of dealing with the intercontinental missile will be produced and developed by the time the Russians have any quantity of the intercontinental missile.
Reference was made to our radar line. I know that those radar lines were designed for and are capable of locating the bomber of today and can be developed to meet the bomber of the next few years. They are not designed to meet the intercontinental missile.
Now, there were a number of other questions which were taken up and I understand that we shall be departing to the other place in the near future and perhaps when we leave this general discussion and get on to the details they can be answered in their proper place.

At this time perhaps I might also take the opportunity to refer to what was said by the gentleman from Alberta. Perhaps he did not mean to cast an aspersion upon the loyalty of the C.C.F. as a group with respect to our national defence, but I would just like to remind him that we have our share of returned veterans and if we, perhaps, are not so vociferous in referring to the bible or the crown that is no reason to infer that we are disloyal or unchristian.
Now what I wanted to speak about in particular had specifically to do with Canadian service colleges. Of course their estimates are scattered throughout many subjects but I do feel that this is the proper time to put my questions. I think it is one of the ironies in connection with education that the only full subsidization of higher education in this country at the present time should be for the purpose of producing soldiers and sailors. Of course, as a believer in full subsidization of higher education so that more people may get the benefit of it, this specific aspect of national defence intrigues me and it seems to me that if the production of regimental officers or air pilots is worthy of full subsidization the same principle should be much more widely extended to cover the training of scientists and specialists in the liberal arts. That of course is something else again.

Supply-National Defence
Now one of the difficulties in there being no breakdown available, and no chance to examine the expenditures in connection with the service colleges and that aspect of the department generally, could be rectified if the minister, in the estimates, the public accounts, or in his departmental report, would provide some facilities for such an examination. That is the first request I would like to make.
The second point I would like to raise is this. A former minister stated there were plans for carrying on the equivalent of postgraduate work for graduates of the service colleges at the national defence college and at the army and air staff colleges. Now in what way is such post graduate work geared to advanced physical research in the fields of missiles, technology and atomic weapons. I would like to know how that is progressing. I have in mind a statement made in 1952 by Mr. Claxton on this very subject. I would also like to know something about the makeup of the advisory board of the Canadian service colleges. Who are the members, and are they still meeting once a year, and has the membership changed? Would the minister say if there has been any great change in the conceptions of the board since his government took office?
Another question I would like to ask, and I know of course that I will have to wait for the minister to obtain expert advice in order to answer me in this respect, is as follows: What is the comparison of costs for the production of officers at each of the three service colleges and what is the comparison of costs between producing an officer at a service college compared to an officer produced under the university training plan? I think these are all aspects of the departmental estimates which we should be entitled to investigate.
Now has there been any discussion about narrowing the rather liberal kind of education now available to students at service colleges? In the first two years especially the education in general is quite liberal and I would like to know if there have been any discussions about narrowing that education and making it more specifically military?
Another question I would like to ask is whether there is a provincial quota for the service colleges and if so have those quotas been filled in recent years and by what provinces?
Further, in 1952 there was an announcement made that the College Militaire in Quebec would have an objective of enrolment of 400 students. I would like to know if that objective has been reached and, if it has not what difficulty stands in the way?

I also have a similar question in connection with the rather different position with respect to the academic professorial staff in the service colleges and similar staffs at the universities. I would like to know whether there is a definite minimum and maximum in terms of pupil load and lecturing hours for the academic staff at service colleges. I have received some reports that such staff is overworked and other reports that they have practically a year-round holiday.
I would further like to know the position of the civilian teaching staff at the service colleges with respect to work in vacation time. For example, could an engineering professor take on private services for a fee or could an arts professor, who had published a book as a result of his studies carried on as an employee of the civil service, have the profits of the publication accrue to him?
Something else I would like to know is how the schedule of salaries for professorial staff in service colleges compares with that recommended by the association of university professors or with that of the University of Toronto which, I understand, is the general standard in Canada by which other colleges and universities govern themselves?
Another question I would like to ask is, can academic civil servants of the department belong to the professorial association of university professors; have they that right?
I would like to know the relationship between the National Council of Canadian Universities and the directors of the Canadian Service Colleges? Just what is the liaison between these groups and are the service colleges part of that national council?
More particularly, how many service college graduates in the last three school years have chosen to go on to take the degree at our universities immediately they were able to do so?
As a penultimate question I would like to ask what is the percentage of Canadian service college graduates which remains in the active forces after completing the term of service? Lastly, what percentage of the student body presently enrolled in the service colleges is, or could be, classified as French Canadian?
I realize, in reading this long list of questions, that it will take time to answer them and that there will be difficulties involved in doing so. I feel, however, that this is the place to ask rather than on the orders of the day and will look forward to sending over this list to the minister and later on, as the discussion continues, to having such answers as his assistants may be able to provide.

I have just a very few questions at this time, Mr. Chairman, but as the night progresses I will have more to add. I would first like to compliment the minister in respect of his announcement than he expects to cut down on the expenses of the department. I may say that I have found him to be one of the most approachable ministers with whom I have ever had contact in this house.
Hear, hear.

I find he is always prepared to meet one and to discuss problems although that does not necessarily mean that I agree with everything that is being done in his particular department. I did hope that we would have had the public accounts of Canada for 1957 by this time so that we could come to some reasonable understanding by a comparison of the estimates for last year with the amounts actually expended by the various departments. My reason for this hope is that I find this is one department in which there is a great discrepancy between the estimates and the actual expenditures.
The people in this country complain bitterly about excessive taxation to which we are subjected and I must under the circumstances refer to the public accounts of Canada for the year 1956 and in particular to volume I, page N-4, to illustrate my particular point.
The estimates set down by the department under departmental administration amounted to $3,494,080 while the amount actually expended was approximately half a million dollars less; $500,000 on an expenditure of some $3 million. Actually, the figure expended was $2,963,787. That represents a difference of about one-sixth, or 16 per cent.
Now I have taken time in the course of the day to review former public accounts and in many instances I have found a similar story. I have tried to discover by going through the estimates exactly where the discrepancy arises. I must say at this point that I do recognize the fact that the minister is new to this particular department and has not had the opportunity of checking these things for himself. He has not had the time. I know how much time it would take to check every individual item among the thousands of items which appear. The point I wish to make is, possibly, best illustrated on page 313 of the estimates for 1957-58 with which we are particularly concerned. I would direct the minister's attention to the section entitled departmental administration.
We see there, under the description of civil staff-possibly civil servants-one deputy minister, one associate deputy minister, three assistant deputy ministers-two at $12,000 and one at $10,500-making in all a total, together 96698-1234
Supply-National Defence with their staffs, of 774 employees in the administrative staff compared with 776 last year. Now the question I have in mind is this: have these offices ever been filled at any one time, all of them, or have any been vacant for a year? Is it the intention of the department to fill these vacancies?
Again, I wish to say that all this points to the fact that we should have a special committee to study these estimates in the same way as other departmental estimates are studied. I could make some very pointed comments about this matter, but I do not intend to pursue the discussion very far at this moment. But if we do have each of these particular offices filled, I am wondering who are the individuals who fill them. As I said, in 1956 there was a discrepancy of over half a million dollars according to the public accounts. Certainly, under "Administration", this is an item identical with the one we find included in the estimates this year.
We find a saving of half a million, which would indicate that the department is expecting the taxpayers of Canada to pay half a million more each year than is actually required, because, to the best of my knowledge, I have never seen all the posts in this department filled at any one time. Possibly the minister would make a statement on this matter later.
I found, also, among other things, a matter which might best be described by reference to the white sheet at the back of the estimates. Let us take one example: construction or acquisition of buildings and works, including land. Hon. members will find that this year we are being asked to appropriate approximately $143 million as compared with $191 million last year, a saving of about $50 million. I should not say it is a saving; we are probably spending $50 million less on buildings. We are just not spending the money. It does seem that at this time we should be better advised to spend the full $191 million on new buildings, not only because we need the buildings but because this is one way of getting .people to work.
While I am dealing with this particular question I wonder if the minister would indicate to the house whether there is any change in policy involved here. Are there to be fewer replacements of armouries? What is the decision of the department? In the city which I have the honour to represent we have an armoury which has been in existence for many years. The building is in very poor condition. Ten years or more ago the former government promised that they would replace this armoury. This was long before my time as a member of parliament, but I remember reading about it in the newspaper. This

Supply[DOT]-National Defence promise has never been fulfilled; there was always one excuse or another, and it seems that the appropriation was never there. If these moneys are not expended and the taxpayer has paid for them, the balance must have appeared at some place in the appropriation. What has happened to this particular balance? Is it being held, is it the intention of the department to carry on a building program or has it other plans. I am sure that each of the hon. members of the house who has an armoury in his area, replacement or renewal of which has been promised, would be very interested to hear the minister's observations on this.
There is another question which I think is very important at this time, and it arises out of a statement made by the Minister of Public Works last evening when he was introducing his housing legislation. If I recall the matter correctly, he indicated that the mari-times and British Columbia were not in a position to take advantage of housing loans. There may be several reasons for this situation, but it could be that these regions are suffering severely from unemployment and as a result the people do not have sufficient money available to make down payments. I find, on checking the loans made in various parts of Canada, that in the province of British Columbia we received only one per cent of the defence orders placed by the federal government. We represent eight per cent of the population, yet we received only one per cent of all defence orders. This is a depressed area, as the hon. member for Vancouver South has very recently found out, as has his colleague the member for Vancouver Centre-
Better get your constituencies straight.

No, I am going right through the list. They have all learned about it by now, including the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. They all know about the condition of the province and the serious unemployment problem. The same applies to the maritimes.	.
What is Mr. Bennett doing about it?
We are building roads and highways and spending every available dollar in the treasury which is a lot more than this government is doing.
What is Saskatchewan doing about it?

If I may continue, sir, I would add that in circumstances such as these where the Department of National Defence has had all these extra dollars appropriated to it and available in the treasury a good place to
(Mr. Hahn.]
spend that money would be in British Columbia and the maritimes and any other areas where there is a serious unemployment problem at this time in order to set those people at work producing some of the articles that are required in carrying out the defence of our country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I assume that we have now concluded the general discussion on this vote?

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make. I would have made them this afternoon but unfortunately I had to be absent to attend the meeting of the external affairs committee.
First of all I must congratulate the minister on his appointment and wish him well in all he undertakes for revision. I think every one realizes that this is one of the most difficult portfolios to deal with in these most uncertain circumstances.
I was interested this morning in the minister's reference to the history of the militia, how it was based on the efforts of the pioneers to provide for their own defence and the defence of the country and how finally in the first world war it was used as the basis of the contingents that went to France. I know as far as my own constituency is concerned the units in Trail and Nelson have been kept going and training has been undertaken week after week, month after month and year after year by a few devoted persons who undertake this work under quite difficult circumstances, in some cases with little public support because of a lack of understanding and because of a degree of uncertainty as to their status in the light of developments that are likely to occur in the future.
In referring to the militia I personally prefer the term "home defence" under these circumstances and I suggested that its role should first of all be primarily home defence, second civil defence and third it should represent training to take action in the case of disaster in peacetime. I think there is a most worth-while role for the militia if training is undertaken along those three lines and that type of training would appeal to many of the younger men who would be willing to join the militia if there were training of that type.
From my experience as a result of talking to the officers, non-commissioned officers and the rank and file of the units in my district I have learned that you cannot arouse very much interest in training year after year on obsolete anti-aircraft guns which I understand were obsolete some years ago and which do not provide much outlet for interest for young men. Because that sort of training has been continued for some years it has been rather

difficult to encourage young men to join the militia in our district. I suggest that first of all you have to have local support and to have local support you must have the type of program in training which engenders that support and local interest.
I suggest that the best results for the money expended can be obtained, particularly under circumstances such as those which obtain in my area, by basic infantry training in which there is training in basic discipline and the understanding of accepting orders and working together in circumstances of emergency. In addition to that I suggest such training could be coupled with frequent manoeuvres into various parts of the district which could be undertaken at very little cost. In fact, the units in my area have undertaken weekend manoeuvres on two or three occasions under the direction of their C.O's. and they have been very successful indeed. I have talked to a lot of the young chaps who were out on these manoeuvres and they appreciated them very much because they felt they were doing something of significance. In a situation such as ours, particularly in a mountainous territory, I believe it is most necessary that we have a corps of men who are well acquainted with the country, its physical features, topography, geography and that sort of thing. In that way the militia is capable of providing a highly adequate home defence in the case of emergency.
Secondly, I think the co-relation of the work of the militia with civil defence can be accomplished with good effect. I was extremely pleased when the minister suggested something more was going to be done in that direction. In fact, if civil defence works in conjunction with the militia I believe we will have a more effective civil defence because there will be a correlation of these two groups both aiming to provide some protection for the country in emergency and in peace.
I also suggest there is an opportunity to use the militia as a group of trained persons willing to be called out to meet any civil disaster in peacetime, particularly during floods and perhaps on occasions when there are very large forest fires when some particularly large organization is required. I stress again my belief that the militia can play a continuing and worth-while role if it is based on home defence, civil defence and disaster defence and alleviation in peacetime.
I am rather parochial in my outlook in some respects because I am essentially a village lad, you know. I feel there is a great deal of value in maintaining the old district names with respect to the militia. There is not much appeal in numbers and that sort
Supply-National Defence of thing but there is a strong appeal in district names and they could be used to a greater extent in any reorganization of the militia. The Rocky Mountain Rangers were formed in the interior of British Columbia in the early days of the century and I remember the drill halls being built in Ross-land, Nelson and Kaslo-I should win the support from the Minister of Public Works in this respect-and in other places and I also recall the interest taken in the militia at that time in an entirely different world situation.
The men who were trained there, like others who were trained in the militia, formed a ready nucleus for the overseas forces during the war. The famous 54 Kootenay regiment was based on the Rocky Mountain Rangers and rendered great service during the first world war. I suggest that the Minister of National Defence would be well advised to form a Kootenay regiment in the Kootenays with platoons or companies in the various towns in question. By so doing the minister would continue the tradition that has been established since the early days of this century and would attract to the militia the sons or grandsons of men who served in the Rocky Mountain Rangers and of those who served in the Kootenay regiment and whose fathers at various times throughout the years served with the militia and the overseas battalion that was formed from it.
I do urge the minister to give some consideration to that and when he replies I would like to get his response to my suggestion in respect of naming the units in the Kootenays, the Kootenay regiment. I am not talking of the engineers or technical groups, but those who are now known as anti-aircraft regiments. I suggest changing those to an infantry regiment. I think it will create much greater interest and will be more suitable for the development of the type of training that is required in that district and will be of considerably less cost than using this heavy equipment and the training that goes with it.

I should like to make just one or two comments on questions which again involve generalities. First of all may I also congratulate the minister and those associated with defence planning on recognizing for the first time, in some 17 years that I have any knowledge of the armed forces, the necessity for planning flexibility in view of the nature of the defence that we have to make for our country.
I would like to suggest that some of the questions that the minister is going to be confronted with, which were partially covered by his remarks, can be answered when

Supply-National Defence we come to the details of the estimates which we will be giving consideration to in just a moment. To be more specific, I would like to suggest to him that the reserve role which he outlined first of all in so far as it applies to the air force auxiliary units, one that we should have recognized some five years ago, would have to be changed. The reason he gave us was the necessity of carrying out a new role in the interests of civil defence with transport units. Perhaps a more important reason is that our weekend pilots who have done an excellent job with the auxiliary units will undoubtedly in the course of the next few years have some difficulty in flying the very fast jet aircraft on limited flying experience. But I would like to suggest to him that in so far as the use of transport aircraft, the Expediters most currently in use are not a satisfactory type, first of all because of their operational limitations. I would like to suggest to him that the Dakota, which has been the workhorse of the transport units in regular squadrons these past years, should replace the Expediter.
In so far as the reserve militia unit is concerned, I think that most of those who served in the militia, or those in this house who served in the militia, recognize as one member said that certain of our artillery pieces of equipment such as the 25-pounder, while it may be out of date, does nevertheless provide us with the firing power which if used in larger scale operations, will give us the elementary training that we require. What I do suggest to the minister and his department is that while there may be some reduction in the application of reserve units to either fighter squadrons, auxiliary units, transport units or artillery, the militia units, integrated as they may be, and although we may not give them the time with the permanent units at reserve camps as formerly, we should not in any way reduce the number of permanent force liason officers who are associated with them. Otherwise, the basic training which our militia units must carry out with two objects in view, namely replacements in permanent units and association with civil defence, will not be achieved. That purpose can only be carried out with a fairly high level and a very efficient group of permanent force officers who during the past years have been associated with the various regiments.
I do not think we should concern ourselves too much so long as we maintain the high level of training standards which the reserve units are experiencing today. This, of course, can be seriously limited if we do in any

way reduce the association with the permanent units who have assisted with the training in the past.
I should like to say a word to the minister on the long-term suggested plan of integrating some of the common ancillary forces with the permanent forces. I heard an hon. member of the C.C.F. party to my extreme right suggest today that perhaps we should integrate the forces as an entity, not just the ancillary sections, that is to say, administrative, medical or police. I would like to remind the minister and that hon. gentleman who made the suggestion that that is an experience that has been tried by every armed force in the world today and it has failed. I think the identity of the three services is essential. I think what might perhaps be regarded as a trial effort would be to use a common medical service, a common police service and a common accounting service. I think there are actually about six other units which, from the standpoint of the service to the main forces, could be incorporated on a basis which would indeed be of great assistance in saving money in the economy of our permanent forces.
I would like to make a reference to the comment of the minister which suggested that we will have in our permanent force a balanced brigade-three of them, I think. This is something which the armed forces have required for some time. We saw the rather regrettable situation when the emergency force was required for the United Nations. The regiment which was based in Calgary had to steal or beg from whatever source it could and from ancillary units to make up a complete composite brigade. The senior officers of both the air force and the army have maintained for some time that if a brigade is to operate efficiently it must train with its ancillary services, so that they can go into action immediately without having hurried wires or messages sent around the country to make it complete. I think it important, too, in the training of our permanent forces that we carry out as many integrated exercises with the United States forces as it is possible to do. Anyone in this house who suggests that because of integrated training we will become involved in an argument of national security or that the sovereignty of our country is endangered does not recognize the very practical and useful experiences that past exercises have given our own forces. I think the incorporation of our two units, that is to say the common forces, the permanent forces of the United States and Canada, as we are today trying to unify the continental command of the air force, will prove highly beneficial to say the least.

I would like to suggest to the minister that in defence planning as a whole the air members of the air force, again in recognition of the necessity of having a continental defence plan, should meet regularly with their counterparts in order to determine whether the use of our forces-and I refer specifically to aircraft now-is in the best interests of continental defence planning.
We have heard a great deal about the 105. It has been said that within the next five years it will no longer be considered to be a top flight aircraft. It has been said by the best known authorities on modern aircraft, and I am not referring particularly to those who may be in Canada, that it still will surpass anything on the drawing boards today. But even accepting that to be so, I believe that almost immediately we are going to have to give consideration to a new prototype which will provide not necessarily greater speed but greater range. I believe that the air members already carrying out planning duties can best do this in cooperation with the United States air force.
I should like to say a word to the hon. member for Kingston who was so concerned about the problem of filing a flight plan, the identifying of aircraft on radar screens and the time lag that might occur. If the hon. member was at all familiar with the procedure he would realize that it takes only a split second to pick up an aircraft on the screen and have fighter aircraft intercept before an enemy plane reaches the coast, and he would not be nearly so alarmed.
Finally, I should like to say this to the minister. Having regard to the white paper produced by Britain in July of last year, I believe, I think the Canadian government can take credit for the fact that so far as planning for defence is concerned the years ahead, as the minister himself said, have taken a somewhat different trend. It seems to me that this is the first attempt by any government to recognize that a change in the nature as we have planned here to take place involves not only the altered role of our militia units but our contribution to the continental defence of Canada and also, of course, to NATO. I believe that this is a very fine department of government, one into which a great deal of planning has gone, and I hope the minister will take into consideration the questions I have put before him.
Mr. Chairman-

No, I want to say a few words before we proceed with the details. I can assure you that I will be brief. I was attending committees this afternoon and was not able to be in the house for that reason. I am not aware if anyone from the province of New Brunswick has brought up the matter to which I wish to refer. I know the minister has received petitions from towns and cities in New Brunswick and from many different organizations in that province protesting the closing of camp Utopia in my own county and the curtailing of a great deal of the activity which has been carried on at camp Gagetown.
Camp Utopia, which was established in Charlotte county in 1941, has been in use every year since that time. It is true it is a small camp but I believe the minister was misinformed when he was told that it was in poor condition. I have been there several times this year, last year and the year before and I find it is kept in very good repair and is an excellent camp. Those who go there year after year are very pleased with the surroundings. There would only be 70, 80 or 90 local people employed there but this is an area where employment is greatly needed and the closing of the camp only added to the unemployment. The camp was of great benefit particularly to the eastern part of the county, the town of St. George and one or two other smaller places. It was appreciated by one and all and as it has been in operation continuously since 1941 I regret very much that the minister decided it was necessary to close it at this time.
Camp Gagetown has been under construction now for several years. I know from my experience and the discussions I have had with officials of the Department of National Defence that the particular site was selected in order to give the province of New Brunswick an additional payroll which was greatly needed. It has been estimated that the payroll at camp Gagetown would be approximately $15 million a year. I know the Minister of Veterans Affairs will agree with me when I say that payroll was needed in our province. The people there had come to depend on it. They felt they had a permanent establishment which would provide that type of payroll for many years to come.
When the people were notified recently by the Minister of National Defence that activity at camp Gagetown would be greatly curtailed during the coming year, in fact that the number of troops would be cut from 10,000 to 4,000, it was a most alarming thing to the people of that area, particularly in our capital city of Fredericton, in Saint John

Supply-National Defence and the larger towns. It was a great shock to all of us. I might add that it was most noticeable that there was no curtailing of the service in Nova Scotia. The military establishments in that province will carry on as they have in the past. I shall only appeal to the minister to reconsider the decision he has made. I can assure him that we in the province of New Brunswick are greatly in need of the assistance which was provided by camp Gagetown. Up to now that camp has cost close to $100 million. The building program, which was well under way, could have been completed in a short time, but it has also been curtailed.

May I correct the hon. member for Charlotte? He just made the statement that there had been no curtailment of troop establishments in Nova Scotia. Is he not aware that the third R.C.H.A. has been moved to camp Gagetown from camp Debert within the last few weeks?

No, I was not aware of that fact. In the petitions I believe reference was made to the fact that there had been no changes made in the province of Nova Scotia. However, if some part of the army has moved from Nova Scotia to camp Gagetown I feel that is no more than right because at camp Gagetown we have the most modern camp to be found in any part of Canada. I can see no reason why activity there should be curtailed in any way in order to be able to carry on in some other part of the maritime provinces or anywhere within reasonable distance of camp Gagetown which is a modern camp from every standpoint.
I am sure that particular site was selected in order to give New Brunswick a little shot in the arm because it was greatly needed. At this very moment there is a great deal of unemployment there. In my own county not only did we lose camp Utopia but just a couple of months before the closing of that camp we lost a textile mill in Milltown on the international border which had been there for 70 years with the result that about 450 people were out of work. That area today is declared to be a surplus area so far as employment is concerned.
I well remember when there was so much criticism of the suggestion in the Gordon report that those who were not able to make a living in the maritimes could be moved to other areas at government expense. Those who sat in the opposition at that time said that it was a dreadful thing for Mr. Gordon to even consider such an idea. But I note that today those sitting on the government side of the house are prepared to furnish


cash to move these people to some other area. But the question today is, where can they go to find employment? There is a lot of unemployment in all parts of Canada. Before I resume my seat I ask the minister to reconsider the decision he has made and secure a little more knowledge closer to that source because the present situation is a great disappointment to the people there and will cause a great deal more unemployment than we have now. We had depended on camp Gagetown to provide employment and I feel it is a camp that should be maintained permanently at full capacity.

Perhaps I might clear up this point now with regard to camp Gagetown, camp Utopia and the other camps in the Atlantic provinces. As the hon. member will know, camp Gagetown was started two or three years ago with the intention of building permanent barracks for approximately a brigade group. There is no change whatever in that plan and we are moving troops into camp Gagetown just as quickly as we can get the accommodation made.
At that point may I ask the minister a question?
Yes.
Did he not make a statement a short time ago that rather than having 10,000 troops in Gagetown in 1958, we would have only 4,000?

The hon. member is confusing those permanently stationed in camp Gagetown and those which are moved in for a short period of summer training. In the past few years there have been troops moved even from as far as British Columbia to camp Gagetown for a short period of summer training in order that they might train as a division. In the coming year it is not the intention to continue that divisional training but there will be troops training in Gagetown and there will be troops permanently stationed in Gagetown. There will be no reduction in the numbers which will eventually be placed in Gagetown. These troops will be moved from the other Atlantic provinces into Gagetown just as quickly as we can get the accommodation made, particularly the married men's accommodation. If we are moving troops into Gagetown as was originally planned-and that was a decision made not by me but by the previous administration-of course we have to move troops from Utopia also into Gagetown and that has already taken place. But we are looking into the question of Utopia to see whether some other use cannot be made of that camp.

While I am on my feet perhaps I might clear up one or two other points. The hon. member for New Westminster asked whether all the positions detailed under administration were always filled. No; they are not always filled. There is a constant review to see whether or not all these positions are necessary.
Then there was the question of armouries. The whole question of the accommodation for the militia or the reserve forces is under investigation. As I pointed out this morning, before the war we had some 4,000 regulars and about the same number of militia as we have today. Now we have 49,000 regulars and they are serving for a period of three years and then the great majority of them go into civilian life. Hence there is being built up a reserve of well trained men. Hence it is necessary to take a look at the whole question of militia accommodation or armouries as they are sometimes referred to. As soon as a complete survey has been made, the armouries which need replacing will be given consideration and will be proceeded with in those localities where they are most urgently needed.
I should like to thank the hon. member for Kootenay West for his very constructive suggestions with regard to the unit in his area. I should like to assure him that when we get these mobile support columns to which I referred this morning fully organized, a sub-unit will carry out one or some of the duties to which he referred. I think those are the main points.

I had not intended to say anything at this stage until the minister mentioned the armouries. I had the estimates here waiting until the item was reached. However, in view of the fact that he has just mentioned the subject, I think probably I should say a word now. I do not know that there would be any reason for my saying anything were it not for the report appearing in the press this evening. I was not here this morning. I was obliged to be at the banking and commerce committee and therefore did not hear what the minister had to say. In the report that is given in this evening's Journal I notice item No. 5 says:
5. The construction program has been reviewed and a number of lower priority items have been deferred.
From previous discussions with the minister I was under the impression, and have so conveyed the message to those at Melville where one of those armouries was intended to be constructed, that the whole plan was under consideration, and I would so understand from the remarks just made. But this report would give the impression that only
Supply-National Defence some of them have been deferred and that they will be considered, and dealt with, I presume, at a later date. I was wondering whether the minister would make a further statement with regard to the proposed armoury at Melville so that it will be more clearly understood by the people there.
Before sitting down I want to join with the others who have congratulated the minister upon having taken over the ministry of defence recently. There is perhaps no one in the house who has had a wider experience in the armed forces of Canada than has the present minister. For that reason many of those on the prairies who have been associated with him will wish me to congratulate him upon having attained his present position.

I thank the right hon. member for Melville for his kind remarks. May I say how much I appreciate his interest in the local militia unit at Melville. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
listened with interest to the minister's remarks this morning, particularly that portion of them which dealt with a matter concerning which we have been trying to get information both here and in another place. When I say "another place", I do not mean the place that is usually referred to in that way but rather the meetings of the committee on external affairs. As I say, I listened to what the minister said this morning about the North American Air Defence command. I am fully aware of the positive assurances that have been given to us that the civilian authority is in ultimate control so far as NORAD is concerned. I am aware of the fact that in due course there may be something in the nature of an exchange of notes on an agreement between this country and the United States that can be made public. In other words, I am not asking the minister to go over the ground that he has been over several times. But it seems to some of us that there are one or two points concerning which we have the right to have information now. These are questions which have been asked here and they have also been asked in the committee on external affairs, but some of us feel that we have not yet been given the answers.
We understand that Air Marshall Slemon has been appointed deputy commander in chief of the Canada-United States air defence command by order in council P.C. 1957/1033 of July 31, 1957. What concerns some of us is the legal constitution of that air defence

Supply-National Defence command. It is one thing to appoint an officer to a position in a command, but how did the command get constituted? We should also like to know the basis on which General Partridge was appointed to be commander in chief of that same Canada-United States air defence command.
So far as Canada is concerned, the only documents we have with regard to this matter are the order in council to which I have just referred and the joint press release put out by the minister and his counterpart in the United States on August 1. These two documents are contained in sessional paper 183 and I would like to ask if the minister knows of any similar documents in the United States appointing General Partridge to his position, or constituting this joint air command? As the minister knows, when General Norstad was in Ottawa speaking to the press and at various places, he made it clear that his authority as a military commander in Europe was derived from the NATO council. In other words, the military was under the civil authority. We know how that authority, namely the NATO council is constituted, and what we are trying to get is the corresponding information regarding the North American air defence command. We know who are the supreme and deputy commanders; they are General Partridge and Air Marshal Slemon. We know that they have been appointed to the command and we have documents telling us about their appointment, but we have no documents telling us about the constituting of the command itself.
Now let me be very frank with the minister and say that these are questions we asked this afternoon in the committee on external affairs and we were told that they were really questions which should be addressed to the Department of National Defence. I hope the minister of this department will not send us back to the other department again. We feel that it is desirable to have this matter cleared up.
The minister has made it clear today, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that the civil authority is in control but we would like to know the constitutional or legal basis of that civil control over the Canada-United States joint air defence command.

I would say that this legal control to which the hon. member has referred will be definitely drawn up and included in the formal note by which we set up this air command. We considered it desirable that the two commanders, General Partridge and Air Marshal Slemon, get together and get working as a team, to discuss this matter between themselves and refer back to their respective governments. The actual formal

note is agreed upon when all the details have been worked out and there will be no doubt that the authority will rest with the civil governments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is
it fair to assume then, in view of the importance of that formal note between the two governments, that it will be drawn in such terms-in other words, leaving out the elements of security-so that the note may be tabled here and also tabled in the appropriate place in the United States?

I would hope that that would be the case. I say I would hope because naturally we are dealing with another government and we would have to get the consent of that government before tabling it. So I say I would hope it would be drawn up in such terms that there would be no doubt that it could be tabled.

Mr. Chairman, I was very pleased to hear the minister say that armouries were going to be replaced according to need. I should like to review for the minister's benefit some of the background on recent events with regard to the proposed armouries for the Irish Regiment which is a reserve unit in Vancouver.
This unit was promised a new armoury in 1914, and the promise has been renewed periodically ever since. They are presently training in a frame building which has been condemned for 20 years. The city recently completed arrangements with the Department
Supply-National Defence of National Defence and turned over to the department some 10 acres of land in the southeast corner of the city in return for three acres of a park called Grandview park owned by the Department of National Defence. It was considered that this proposed location was ill advised and unsuitable, and a fight was led to try to stop the building of the armoury at that location. The location was in the middle of a single family dwelling area. It had no public transportation; the nearest bus line would be about a quarter of a mile away, and had a frequency of service of around twice an hour. The militia was not happy with the location, but they had been waiting since 1914 and were willing to take anything.
The arrangement had been that the city of Vancouver would operate a police training academy on the same land and in buildings separate from the armoury. Eventually the police commission decided to switch the police training academy to the Pacific National Exhibition grounds and the city council reversed their plans with regard to the location of this armoury.
The present situation is that the department and the city first of all agreed on the location in an area, which, as I said, was not suitable for an armoury. Now communications have, I believe, emanated from the city to the department asking for a review of this armoury question and its location in a more suitable area.
The modern thinking with regard to an armoury is that it should be located in a well-populated area and should draw its recruits from that area. That would mean a higher priced parcel of land, because the area which has been under consideration is in an undeveloped section, very thinly settled and, in fact, the only area left in Vancouver suitable for large scale subsidized housing development, homes for pensioners and so on. The whole question involves the need to reopen communications between the department and the city so that a more suitable location may be found and the way cleared for the building of this armoury.
An armoury is required by the unit, but the present location is not suitable and I should like the minister, when he has the chance, to have his staff follow this matter up so that it does not become bogged down, and discuss with the city council the new situation which has arisen so that suitable land may be acquired and the armoury built.

Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to ask a question to clarify something in my mind. I notice that the Minister of National Defence in his reply to the hon. member for

Another question, Mr. Chairman. The minister asked us this morning if we would speak about as much on the general discussion as we could and I am sure we all want to co-operate and not speak too long on individual items other than those particular ones we want to ask about. The minister showed us how he spent an extra $41 million, by a $34 million increase in pay and allowances and another expenditure of $7 million on the mid-Canada line. He also stated that he had decreased spending in the department by about the equivalent amount of $41 million. I would ask the minister, in order that the members may more intelligently put a spending tag after each item, if he could give us a statement detailing his decreases in expenditure and naming the item to which each decrease would be applied. I think it will be easier for the members then to go over the items and know what they are talking about -what is still on the estimate, and if there has been a reduction what item is reduced.

I gave the general area in which reductions have taken place in the remarks I made this morning. To go over every item now would take a very long time, and it would be necessary for me to have my officials here with their lists of items that have been reduced. There have been reductions made in a large number of different items.

Why I ask that of the minister is that there are a multitude of items and if he could tell us ahead of time, then we would not have to ask on these items: is this item reduced. If he would provide us with this statement-surely, there will be sufficient time overnight-or if he would make some arrangement whereby we could be told what items were reduced, time might be saved. If not it might occur to some members to ask whether this or that item was reduced, and this type of statement might eliminate that type of questioning. Or we might think we have something on the estimates which the [DOT]uinister has erased altogether, because he


has not told us in particular about each item. I am sure that having reduced the estimates by $41 million he must have some kind of statement available he could attach to the various items or make an appendix to our proceedings.
Yes, I have a statement. When we have passed this first item and can get my officials in here they have a statement which goes into more detail.

The hon. member will realize, of course, that there are different officials dealing with different branches-different officials dealing with the navy, the air force and the army. It is hard to get them all here around one small table.

I agree with the minister, but I think he will agree with me that perhaps no other department of government which presents estimates to the House of Commons has such a small number of items in relation to the dollars involved. I think, in consequence, that if he has changes to make, he could, in deference to the hon. members of this house who do not divide themselves up into categories of air force, navy and army, assist them by providing some form of breakdown of the reductions he is prepared to stand by, compared with the gross items which appear before us.
I appreciate the hon. member's difficulty because I remember when I was sitting on the other side of the house I encountered exactly the same problem-

Mr. Chairman, in rising at
this time I would like to express agreement with much of the discussion that has taken place this afternoon but there is one point I feel we have overlooked. In any event it has been troubling me and I believe it is of concern to many people in this country.
When we look at the total estimated expenditures for national defence we find they amount to approximately $4,866 million for this year. The minister said that one-third of the tax dollar will go toward defence. This is most interesting because our taxes have increased considerably since 1949. Whereas in that year we were paying a per capita tax of $160 we find it has risen today to approximately $325 per person.

Supply-[DOT]National Defence Out of every dollar earned by people in Canada almost 25 cents goes into the federal treasury in the form of taxes. In view of this heavy taxation and our huge defence expenditures one cannot help but wonder sometimes, particularly in the light of certain press reports which appear from time to time, if we are getting our dollar's worth in terms of goods and services for every dollar we spend.

These projects which commenced a little over a year ago have now been abandoned. Mr. Chairman, I listened very closely to what the minister had to say and he has not answered my argument at all. In fact, we are farther apart on this than we were before. In 1955 there was no general election and in 1956 we appropriated the sum of $3,494,080, as indicated on page N-4 of the public accounts for that year.
The actual expenditure was $2,963,000. That was just for administration. The fact is that the saving apparently arose because we did not have as many on the civil staff as had been appropriated for. The same thing held true the year before and the year before that and I do not think elections had anything to do with it. It does not seem to have anything to do with it in view of the comparative figures as I go through the public accounts from one department to another. I must say I have been doing some homework. For that reason I say that with respect to administration the department could apparently save $28 million in civil staff wages alone.
I do know the minister indicated that there was going to be a reduction of $380,000 and I think he broke it down into postage, $20,000, and so on, but he did not indicate anything with respect to the civil staff and there must be some considerable saving there. I have a great deal of faith in the minister. I have known him for a number of years and I am satisfied he will look into the matter before another year but it is a matter of great concern. I am satisfied in my own mind, and it has not been proven otherwise up to now, that we are overestimating the dollars we require for the civil staff. It is not that we are going to have any more unemployed because I am not suggesting we should get rid of anybody. It is just that we are appropriating funds for civil staff and then never filling all the positions.

All I can say to that is that there is a constant review of the requirements going on. That practice has been in effect for years and it is still being continued. I hope that when the next estimates, which will be prepared by the present government,

Supply-National Defence are presented next year they will show that the same practice is continuing.

There is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and it would seem that this would be the appropriate item on which to raise it. They have based their application on legislation which provides that active service by a person in any of the naval or army forces of 'Newfoundland or by a person who was recruited in Newfoundland for any naval, army or air forces raised in Newfoundland by or on behalf of the United Kingdom shall be deemed to be active service in the Canadian forces. Supply-National Defence

subtopic: WINTER NAVIGATION STUDIES, LAKEHEAD
WINTER NAVIGATION STUDIES, LAKEHEAD
speechtext:
1.	Have any preliminary studies been made of the problems in keeping the Canadian lakehead harbours open through the winter?
2.	If so, could such studies be summarized to indicate the feasibility of the matter?
3.	To the government's knowledge, have American authorities made any studies or plans with regard to the possibility of keeping the American Soo locks open in the winter?
Answer by: Mr. MacDonald, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Transport:
1.	The department has continually under review the question of improved methods of dealing with winter navigation in Canada. Programs involved range from development of icebreaking capabilities to studies of various technical experiments. All of these are of general applicability rather than related to any one port. In the case of the lakehead, the next most useful step will be the experience gained when the department's new great

lakes vessel, which is being built to icebreaker standards, comes into service and is available at the lakehead for use, in about 12 to 18 months' time.
2.	Answered by No. 1 above.
3.	It is understood that the United States authorities have performed a number of experiments regarding the keeping of the locks open under winter conditions, but the department is not aware of any definite decisions or plans by the United States authorities to keep the United States locks open for any specific winter period.

subtopic: DREDGING WORK, LOWER FRASER RIVER
DREDGING WORK, LOWER FRASER RIVER
speechtext:
1.	Was certain dredging work carried out on the lower Fraser river between Tree island and the mainland (north side) or Lulu island during the past summer? If so, who authorized the work?
2.	Was there a time limit on the project? If so, what date was the work to commence and terminate?
3.	What was the purpose of the project?
4.	Has the work been completed according to plan? If not, what is its present position?
5. Where were the dredging spoils from this project deposited, and by whose direction?
6.	Has such fill material any monetary value in this area? If so, how much was received from its sale?
7.	Was any crown land, either provincial or federal, requiring fill within a convenient deposit distance of this project?
8.	Was any payment offered on a quantity basis for dredging spoils deposited on private land within dumping distance of this project at anv time since February 1, 1957? If so, who made the offer and on what terms?
Answer by:	Mr. Hodgson, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Public Works:
1.	Dredging was carried out on the lower Fraser river between Tree island and the north side of Lulu island. This work was carried out by plant owned by the Department of Public Works who authorized the work.
2.	This project was part of the schedule of work to be done by dredge P.W.D. No. 322 during the 1957 dredging season and no fixed dates were established for commencement or completion.
3.	The purposes of this project are to block the upper end of the channel between Tree and Lulu islands and thus reduce dredging in the main channel above the block; to dredge out and improve the channel between Tree and Lulu islands below the block for all the holders of riparian rights adjacent to it.
4.	Work has been virtually completed according to plan.
5.	The spoil from this project was deposited in the provincial crown land located in the channel between the end of Tree island and Lulu island. Some surplus spoil was deposited on private land located adjacent to this spoil area.
Questions
6.	The spoil has no monetary value in so far as the federal government is concerned and the spoil was not sold.
7.	Provincial crown land requiring fill located in the channel between Tree island and Lulu island was used as a spoil area. Some surplus spoil was placed on private land adjacent to this crown land.
8.	No payment was offered on a quantity basis for dredging spoils deposited on private land within a distance that could be serviced by equipment owned by the Department of Public Works.
